subtopics.title: Kirchhoff's Laws & Network Theorems
subtopics.subtitle: KCL, KVL, circuit vocabulary, nodal and mesh analysis, and a map of the theorems

concepts.text: Kirchhoff's Laws

KCL: the algebraic sum of currents at any node is zero (charge conservation). KVL: the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero (energy conservation). Ohm's law alone cannot solve a circuit with several loops or several sources; Kirchhoff's two laws supply the extra equations, and every network theorem in this topic is ultimately derived from them.
Circuit vocabulary used in every theorem:
items: Node: a point where two or more elements are joined. A principal node (junction) joins three or more branches.
Branch: a single element, or several elements in series, between two nodes; one current per branch.
Loop: any closed path through the circuit that passes no node more than once.
Mesh: a loop that encloses no other loop, the 'window panes' of a planar circuit.
Independent equations: a circuit with n nodes and b branches yields n − 1 KCL equations and b − n + 1 KVL (mesh) equations.

concepts.text: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)

Statement: the sum of currents entering a node equals the sum of currents leaving it; algebraically ΣI = 0 at every node. Principle: conservation of charge, because charge cannot accumulate at a junction. Sign convention: count currents entering as positive and currents leaving as negative (or the reverse), but use one rule for the whole node. A current whose direction was guessed wrongly simply comes out negative in the solution.

concepts.plainText: ΣI_in = ΣI_out at every node

concepts.text: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)

Statement: the algebraic sum of all voltages (source EMFs and element drops) around any closed loop is zero, ΣV = 0. Principle: conservation of energy, since a charge carried once round a closed path returns to its starting potential. Sign convention: walk round the loop in one direction; passing through an element from − to + is a voltage rise and is taken positive, passing from + to − is a voltage drop and is taken negative. For a resistor the drop is IR in the direction of the current, so the loop equation is often written as sum of EMFs = sum of IR drops.

concepts.plainText: ΣV(loop) = 0, i.e. ΣE = ΣIR

concepts.text: Nodal and Mesh Analysis
Two systematic methods built directly on Kirchhoff's laws:
items: Nodal analysis (KCL): pick a reference node (0 V), label the other node voltages, write KCL at each non-reference principal node with branch currents expressed as (V_a − V_b)/R, and solve. Current sources enter directly; a voltage source between two nodes fixes their difference.

Mesh analysis (KVL): assign a clockwise current to each mesh, write KVL round every mesh (a resistor shared by two meshes carries the difference of their mesh currents) and solve the simultaneous equations. Voltage sources enter directly; a current source fixes the current of the mesh it lies in.
A branch current is a mesh current or the difference of two; an element voltage is a node voltage or the difference of two.
Choose the method with fewer unknowns: n − 1 node voltages versus b − n + 1 mesh currents.

concepts.text: Source Transformation

A practical voltage source V_s in series with R_s behaves, at its terminals, exactly like a current source I_s = V_s/R_s in parallel with the same R_s, and vice versa; a load cannot tell them apart. The arrow of the current source points toward the terminal that is positive in the voltage-source form. Repeated transformations can collapse a ladder network into a single loop. Ideal sources (R_s = 0 for a voltage source, R_s = ∞ for a current source) have no equivalent and cannot be transformed.
Network Theorems
The theorems examiners love:
items: Thevenin's: any linear two-terminal network reduces to one voltage source V_th in series with a resistance R_th.
Norton's: the same network as one current source I_N in parallel with R_N (R_N = R_th, I_N = V_th/R_th).
Superposition: the response equals the algebraic sum of the responses to each independent source acting alone (the others replaced by their internal resistance).
Maximum power transfer: the load receives maximum power when R_L = R_th; the maximum power is V_th²/4R_th.

rows: Algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero (charge conservation)
Algebraic sum of voltages round a closed loop is zero (energy conservation)

One load varies; find its V or I quickly
Linear two-terminal network = I_N (short-circuit current) in parallel with R_N = R_th

V_s in series with R ⇔ I_s = V_s/R in parallel with R

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Kirchhoff's Laws and Systematic Analysis

Why only n − 1 KCL equations? Every branch current leaves one node and enters another, so if the KCL equations of all n nodes are added, every current appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign and the sum is identically zero. One node equation is therefore always a combination of the others, and it is dropped by making that node the reference. In graph terms a tree joins all n nodes with n − 1 twigs; each of the remaining b − n + 1 links closes exactly one independent loop, which is why that many KVL equations are needed.

concepts.plainText: [G][V] = [I_s]: G_kk = sum of conductances at node k; G_kj = −(conductance between k and j)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: nodal analysis with two unknown nodes
Circuit: 20 V source behind 4 Ω feeds node A; A to ref 4 Ω;
A to B 2 Ω; B to ref 8 Ω; 3 A current source into B.
KCL at A: (20 − VA)/4 = VA/4 + (VA − VB)/2
          → 5 = VA(0.25 + 0.25 + 0.5) − 0.5 VB = VA − 0.5 VB
KCL at B: 3 + (VA − VB)/2 = VB/8
          → 3 = −0.5 VA + 0.625 VB
From the first: VA = 5 + 0.5 VB
Substitute: 3 = −2.5 − 0.25 VB + 0.625 VB → VB = 5.5/0.375 = 14.67 V
VA = 5 + 7.33 = 12.33 V
Check at A: (20 − 12.33)/4 = 1.92 A in; 12.33/4 + (12.33 − 14.67)/2
            = 3.08 − 1.17 = 1.92 A out  ✓

When a voltage source joins two non-reference nodes, its current cannot be written as (V_a − V_b)/R. Enclose both nodes in a supernode, write one KCL equation for the whole enclosure, and add the constraint V_a − V_b = V_s. The dual situation in mesh analysis is a current source shared by two meshes: its voltage is unknown, so KVL is written round the supermesh that bypasses it, with the constraint that the difference of the two mesh currents equals the source current.

Worked example 2: mesh analysis (both mesh currents clockwise)
Mesh 1: 30 V source, 3 Ω, shared 6 Ω.  Mesh 2: shared 6 Ω, 4 Ω, 2 Ω.
Mesh 1: 30 = 3 I1 + 6(I1 − I2) = 9 I1 − 6 I2
Mesh 2:  0 = 6(I2 − I1) + 4 I2 + 2 I2 = −6 I1 + 12 I2  → I1 = 2 I2
Substitute: 30 = 18 I2 − 6 I2 = 12 I2 → I2 = 2.5 A, I1 = 5 A
Shared 6 Ω carries I1 − I2 = 2.5 A (direction of I1), drop = 15 V
KVL check, mesh 2: 15 V = 2.5 × (4 + 2) = 15 V  ✓
Power check: source 30 × 5 = 150 W; resistors
  5²×3 + 2.5²×6 + 2.5²×4 + 2.5²×2 = 75 + 37.5 + 25 + 12.5 = 150 W  ✓

rows: Current source shared by two meshes (supermesh)

concepts.text: In AC circuits KCL and KVL hold at every instant, so they also hold for phasors, but not for RMS magnitudes. Two currents of 3 A and 4 A that are 90° apart combine to 5 A, not 7 A, and three equal voltages 120° apart add to zero. Add the phasors (or the instantaneous values) first and take the magnitude last.
Common mistakes in KCL/KVL problems:
items: Changing the sign convention half-way round a loop or node; fix one rule for rises and drops and keep it.
Writing only one mesh current for a shared resistor instead of the difference I₁ − I₂.
Treating a negative answer as an error; it only means the assumed direction was wrong.
Adding RMS magnitudes of AC currents at a node as if they were in phase.
Transforming an ideal source, or using the transformed model to find the power lost inside the source.

concepts.text: Before solving, count: n − 1 node equations versus b − n + 1 mesh equations, and pick the smaller set. After solving, do a power balance (total power delivered = total power absorbed); it catches most sign errors in seconds.

formulas.plainText: Sum of node currents = 0; sum of loop voltages = 0
ΣE = ΣIR round any closed loop (KVL)
I_s = V_s / R_s, same R_s moved from series to parallel

notes.text: KCL goes with conservation of Charge, KVL with conservation of energy (Voltage). Examiners swap them deliberately; the C in KCL is the reminder.
In mesh analysis a resistor shared by two meshes carries the difference of the two mesh currents. Writing only one of them is the classic sign error that makes every later answer wrong.

Source transformation preserves everything seen at the terminals but not what happens inside the source: the power dissipated in R_s is different in the two forms, so transform only the part of the circuit you do not need to look inside.

formulas.title: Kirchhoff's current law
formulas.description: At any node the currents entering equal the currents leaving; use it to write node equations.

formulas.title: Kirchhoff's voltage law
formulas.plainText: ΣV = 0 round a loop, i.e. ΣE = ΣIR
formulas.description: Round any closed loop the rises (EMFs) equal the drops (IR); use it to write loop or mesh equations.

formulas.title: Source transformation
formulas.description: A voltage source V_s in series with R_s equals a current source I_s in parallel with the same R_s; arrow toward the + terminal.

formulas.title: Number of independent equations
formulas.plainText: KCL equations = n − 1; KVL equations = b − n + 1
formulas.description: For a circuit with n nodes and b branches; tells you how many node or mesh equations you must write.

flashcards.front: Which conservation law underlies KCL, and which underlies KVL?
flashcards.back: KCL: conservation of charge (no charge piles up at a node). KVL: conservation of energy (a charge carried round a closed loop returns to its starting potential).

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a loop and a mesh?
flashcards.back: A loop is any closed path; a mesh is a loop that encloses no other loop. Mesh analysis writes KVL only round the meshes.

flashcards.front: Convert a 12 V source with 4 Ω series resistance into a current source.
flashcards.back: I_s = 12/4 = 3 A in parallel with the same 4 Ω, arrow pointing toward the former + terminal.

flashcards.front: When would you choose nodal analysis instead of mesh analysis?
flashcards.back: When the circuit has fewer (n − 1) node voltages than (b − n + 1) mesh currents, or when it contains current sources, which enter KCL equations directly.

questions.questionText: At a junction, currents of 5 A and 3 A flow in, a current of 2 A flows out, and one more branch carries an unknown current I out of the junction. What is I?
questions.explanation: KCL: current in = current out, so 5 + 3 = 2 + I, giving I = 6 A.

questions.questionText: A 60 V supply feeds three resistors of 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω connected in parallel. Using KCL at the supply terminal, the total current drawn from the supply is:
questions.explanation: Branch currents are 60/10 = 6 A, 60/20 = 3 A and 60/30 = 2 A; by KCL the supply current is 6 + 3 + 2 = 11 A.

questions.questionText: A connected planar network has 6 nodes and 9 branches. How many independent mesh (KVL) equations does it need?
questions.explanation: Independent KVL equations = b − n + 1 = 9 − 6 + 1 = 4. The value 5 is n − 1, the number of node equations.

questions.questionText: Nodal analysis is applied to a circuit that has 5 principal nodes. How many node-voltage equations must be written?
questions.explanation: One node is chosen as the reference (0 V), so only n − 1 = 5 − 1 = 4 node voltages are unknown and 4 KCL equations are needed.

questions.questionText: A 5 A ideal current source in parallel with a 10 Ω resistor is converted by source transformation. The equivalent is:
options: 50 V source in series with 10 Ω
0.5 V source in series with 10 Ω
50 V source in parallel with 10 Ω
2 V source in series with 10 Ω
questions.explanation: V_s = I_s × R = 5 × 10 = 50 V, and the same 10 Ω is moved from parallel to series.

questions.questionText: A 24 V source drives a single loop containing resistors of 2 Ω, 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series. The voltage across the 4 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: I = 24/(2 + 4 + 6) = 2 A, so V_4Ω = 2 × 4 = 8 V. By KVL the other drops (4 V + 12 V = 16 V) make up the rest of the 24 V.

questions.questionText: Going round a closed loop, you pass two EMFs of 12 V and 5 V, both as rises, a resistor drop of 8 V and an unknown drop V_x. By KVL, V_x equals:
questions.explanation: Sum of rises = sum of drops: 12 + 5 = 8 + V_x, so V_x = 9 V.

questions.questionText: Kirchhoff's voltage law is a statement of the conservation of:
questions.explanation: A charge taken once round a closed path returns to the same potential, so the net work done on it is zero; KVL therefore expresses conservation of energy. KCL is the law based on conservation of charge.

questions.questionText: In circuit analysis, a mesh is best defined as:
options: Any closed path in the circuit
A point where three or more branches meet
A path between two adjacent nodes
A loop that does not enclose any other loop
questions.explanation: A mesh is a 'window' of a planar circuit: a loop with no other loop inside it. Every mesh is a loop, but not every loop is a mesh.

questions.questionText: In nodal analysis, the node that is assigned zero potential and against which all other node voltages are measured is called the:
questions.explanation: One node, usually the one with the most branches or the ground, is taken as the reference or datum node at 0 V.

questions.questionText: Which of the following CANNOT be converted by source transformation?
options: A 12 V source in series with 3 Ω
A 2 A source in parallel with 6 Ω
A 9 V source in series with 1 Ω
An ideal voltage source with no series resistance
questions.explanation: Transformation needs a finite, non-zero resistance: I_s = V_s/R_s would be infinite for R_s = 0, so an ideal voltage source has no current-source equivalent.

questions.questionText: Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws are valid for:
options: Both linear and non-linear lumped circuits
questions.explanation: KCL and KVL come from conservation of charge and energy, not from the element laws, so they hold for any lumped circuit, linear or non-linear, DC or AC.

questions.questionText: A branch of an electric circuit is:
options: A closed path that returns to its starting node
A junction of three or more conductors
The reference point of the circuit
A single element, or elements in series, between two nodes
questions.explanation: A branch connects two nodes and carries a single current; a closed path is a loop, and a junction is a principal node.

questions.questionText: Mesh analysis in its standard form can be applied only to circuits that are:
questions.explanation: Meshes are defined as the windows of a circuit drawn flat on a plane, so the method needs a planar circuit. Current sources and AC sources are handled without difficulty.

questions.questionText: Two sinusoidal currents of the same frequency enter a node: 3∠0° A and 4∠90° A (RMS phasors). The only other branch at the node carries the total out. The RMS value of that current is:
questions.explanation: KCL holds for phasors: I = 3∠0° + 4∠90° = 3 + j4 A, so |I| = √(3² + 4²) = 5 A. Adding magnitudes (7 A) ignores the phase difference.

questions.questionText: Currents i₁ = 10 sin ωt A and i₂ = 10 sin(ωt + 120°) A enter a node and leave through a single third branch. The peak value of the current in the third branch is:
questions.explanation: KCL applies instant by instant: i₃ = i₁ + i₂. Adding phasors 10∠0° + 10∠120° = 5 + j8.66, whose magnitude is 10 A. 20 A adds peaks; 17.32 A would be the result for a 60° separation.

questions.questionText: A 12 V source feeds node A through a 6 Ω resistor. A 1 A current source also feeds current into node A, and a 3 Ω resistor connects A to the source's negative terminal (reference). The voltage of node A is:
questions.explanation: KCL at A: (12 − V)/6 + 1 = V/3 → 2 − V/6 + 1 = V/3 → 3 = V/2 → V = 6 V. Ignoring the current source gives 4 V; reversing it gives 2 V.

questions.questionText: A single loop contains a 12 V source and a 4 V source connected in opposition, a 2 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor. The loop current is:
questions.explanation: Opposing EMFs subtract: I = (12 − 4)/(2 + 6) = 8/8 = 1 A. Adding them (16/8 = 2 A) treats the sources as aiding.

questions.questionText: Two practical sources, 12 V with 3 Ω internal resistance and 6 V with 6 Ω internal resistance, are connected in parallel with like terminals together. Using source transformation, the open-circuit terminal voltage is:
questions.explanation: Transform each: 12/3 = 4 A and 6/6 = 1 A, total 5 A in parallel with 3 Ω ∥ 6 Ω = 2 Ω. Open-circuit voltage = 5 × 2 = 10 V. The simple average (9 V) is wrong because the resistances differ.

questions.questionText: An 18 V source in series with 3 Ω feeds node A; a 6 Ω resistor joins A to the reference; from A a 2 Ω resistor leads to a 4 Ω load returning to the reference. Using repeated source transformation, the load current is:
questions.explanation: 18 V/3 Ω → 6 A ∥ 3 Ω; with 6 Ω this is 6 A ∥ 2 Ω → 12 V in series with 2 Ω; add 2 Ω → 12 V behind 4 Ω. I_L = 12/(4 + 4) = 1.5 A. Forgetting the 6 Ω shunt gives 18/9 = 2 A.

questions.questionText: Two series branches are connected across a 20 V supply: branch 1 is 4 Ω (top) then 6 Ω (bottom), and branch 2 is 8 Ω (top) then 2 Ω (bottom). Point a is the junction in branch 1 and point b the junction in branch 2. Taking the bottom rail as reference, V_ab is:
questions.explanation: V_a = 20 × 6/10 = 12 V and V_b = 20 × 2/10 = 4 V. Going from b to a by KVL, V_ab = V_a − V_b = 12 − 4 = 8 V.

questions.questionText: A practical source of 10 V with 2 Ω internal resistance is left open-circuited. Its source-transformed (current-source) model predicts an internal power dissipation of:
questions.explanation: The equivalent is 5 A in parallel with 2 Ω; on open circuit all 5 A flows in the 2 Ω, dissipating 5² × 2 = 50 W, while the voltage-source model dissipates 0 W. Transformation preserves terminal behaviour only, not internal power.

questions.questionText: In a Wheatstone bridge, arm AC = 10 Ω, arm CB = 20 Ω and arm AD = 30 Ω; the supply is across A and B and the galvanometer across C and D. For zero galvanometer current, arm DB must be:
questions.explanation: At balance V_C = V_D, which by KVL requires AC/CB = AD/DB: 10/20 = 30/DB, so DB = 60 Ω.

questions.questionText: In a two-mesh circuit a 12 V source and a 2 Ω resistor lie only in mesh 1, a 4 Ω resistor is shared by meshes 1 and 2, and both mesh currents I₁ and I₂ are taken clockwise. In the KVL equation for mesh 1, the coefficient of I₂ is:
questions.explanation: Mesh 1: 12 = 2I₁ + 4(I₁ − I₂) = 6I₁ − 4I₂. The mutual resistance appears with a minus sign when both mesh currents are clockwise; 6 is the self-resistance (coefficient of I₁).

questions.questionText: Two adjacent meshes share a 5 Ω resistor. Solving the mesh equations gives clockwise mesh currents I₁ = 3 A and I₂ = 1 A. The current in the shared resistor and the voltage across it are:
questions.explanation: Clockwise mesh currents flow in opposite directions through the shared branch, so its current is I₁ − I₂ = 2 A in the direction of I₁, and V = 2 × 5 = 10 V.

questions.questionText: Node voltages found by nodal analysis are V_A = 10 V and V_B = −2 V (relative to the reference). A 4 Ω resistor connects A and B. The current in it is:
questions.explanation: I = (V_A − V_B)/R = (10 − (−2))/4 = 12/4 = 3 A, flowing from the higher potential A to B. Using 10 − 2 gives the wrong 2 A.

questions.questionText: A circuit has 4 nodes and 8 branches. Comparing the number of simultaneous equations, which method is more economical?
options: Mesh analysis: 3 equations against 5 node equations
Nodal analysis: 3 equations against 5 mesh equations
Mesh analysis: 4 equations against 5 node equations
questions.explanation: Node equations = n − 1 = 3; mesh equations = b − n + 1 = 8 − 4 + 1 = 5, so nodal analysis needs fewer equations.

questions.questionText: In the graph of a connected network with n nodes and b branches, a tree contains how many branches (twigs)?
questions.explanation: A tree connects all n nodes without forming a loop, which needs exactly n − 1 twigs. The remaining b − n + 1 branches are links, one for each independent loop equation.

questions.questionText: In nodal analysis, a supernode is formed when:
options: A current source is shared by two meshes
A voltage source is connected between two non-reference nodes
Three or more resistors meet at a node
A node is connected directly to the reference through a wire
questions.explanation: A voltage source between two non-reference nodes hides its current, so the two nodes are enclosed together: one KCL equation is written for the enclosure and the source supplies the constraint V_a − V_b = V_s.

questions.questionText: In mesh analysis, a supermesh is formed when:
options: A voltage source lies on the outer boundary of a mesh
A resistor is shared by two meshes
Two meshes have the same current
A current source lies in a branch shared by two meshes
questions.explanation: The voltage across a current source is unknown, so KVL is written round the combined loop that avoids it, and the source gives the constraint I₂ − I₁ = I_s.

questions.questionText: For a resistive circuit without dependent sources, written in the matrix form [G][V] = [I] for nodal analysis, a diagonal element G_kk equals:
options: The conductance between node k and the reference only
The sum of the conductances connected to node k
The negative of the conductance between node k and its neighbours
The reciprocal of the total resistance of the circuit
questions.explanation: G_kk is the self-conductance, the sum of every conductance meeting at node k; off-diagonal terms G_kj are the negative of the conductance joining nodes k and j, which makes the matrix symmetric.

questions.questionText: After solving a mesh-analysis problem, one mesh current comes out as −2.5 A. This means:
options: An arithmetic error has definitely been made
The actual current is 2.5 A in the direction opposite to that assumed
The mesh contains a source that absorbs power
The current is 2.5 A in the assumed direction but the sources are reversed
questions.explanation: Directions are assumed arbitrarily; a negative answer simply means the true current flows opposite to the assumed direction with magnitude 2.5 A.

questions.questionText: Which statement about Kirchhoff's current law is correct?
options: It applies only to nodes joining exactly three branches
It applies only to DC currents
It applies to any closed surface as well as to a single node
It requires all resistors at the node to be equal
questions.explanation: Because charge cannot accumulate inside any lumped region, the net current crossing any closed surface is zero; this generalised KCL is what justifies the supernode.

questions.questionText: Which statement about Kirchhoff's laws and circuit power is NOT correct?
options: KCL follows from conservation of charge
KVL can be applied to phasor voltages in a sinusoidal steady-state circuit
KVL holds only in circuits supplied by DC sources
The sum of powers absorbed by all elements of a circuit is zero
questions.explanation: KVL is valid at every instant for any lumped circuit, so it also holds for AC voltages and for phasors. The other three statements are true; the last is Tellegen's power balance.

questions.questionText: Kirchhoff's laws in their usual form may fail when:
options: The circuit is supplied by an AC source
The circuit has more than ten branches
The circuit dimensions are comparable to the wavelength of the signal
questions.explanation: KCL and KVL assume a lumped circuit in which signals travel between elements instantaneously. At very high frequencies, when dimensions approach the wavelength, the circuit becomes distributed and transmission-line analysis is required.

questions.questionText: A 20 V source with its positive terminal at terminal a has an internal resistance of 4 Ω. In the equivalent current-source form, the source value and arrow direction are:
options: 5 A with the arrow pointing toward terminal a
5 A with the arrow pointing away from terminal a
80 A with the arrow pointing toward terminal a
0.2 A with the arrow pointing toward terminal a
questions.explanation: I_s = V_s/R_s = 20/4 = 5 A, and the arrow points toward the terminal that is positive in the voltage-source form so that both models push current out of terminal a into a load.

questions.questionText: In nodal analysis, an ideal voltage source is connected between node A and the reference node. The effect on the analysis is that:
options: V_A is known directly, so one fewer KCL equation is needed
Node A must be merged with the reference node
The source must first be converted to a current source
A supermesh must be formed around the source
questions.explanation: The source fixes V_A = V_s, so node A drops out of the unknowns and no KCL equation is written there. A supernode is needed only when the source joins two non-reference nodes; an ideal source cannot be transformed.

questions.questionText: A 16 V source feeds node A through 2 Ω. Node A has a 5 Ω resistor to the reference and a 2 Ω resistor to node B. Node B has a 4 Ω resistor to the reference and a 1 A current source feeding into it. The node voltages V_A and V_B are:
questions.explanation: KCL at A: (16 − V_A)/2 = V_A/5 + (V_A − V_B)/2; KCL at B: 1 + (V_A − V_B)/2 = V_B/4. Solving gives V_A = 10 V, V_B = 8 V (check: 3 A in, 2 A to ground, 1 A to B; at B 1 + 1 = 2 A = 8/4).

questions.questionText: An 8 A current source feeds node A from the reference. A 2 Ω resistor joins A to the reference, and a 10 V source is connected between A (+) and node B, which has a 4 Ω resistor to the reference. The voltage across the 4 Ω resistor and the power delivered by the current source are:
questions.explanation: Supernode A–B: V_A − V_B = 10 and 8 = V_A/2 + V_B/4 → 8 = (V_B + 10)/2 + V_B/4 → V_B = 4 V, V_A = 14 V. Power of current source = 8 × V_A = 8 × 14 = 112 W.

questions.questionText: Mesh 1 contains a 20 V source that drives current clockwise round mesh 1 and a 4 Ω resistor; mesh 2 contains a 6 Ω resistor; the branch shared by the two meshes is a 2 A current source that makes I₂ − I₁ = 2 A (clockwise mesh currents). Using a supermesh, the current in the 6 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: Supermesh KVL round the outer loop: 20 = 4I₁ + 6I₂ with I₂ = I₁ + 2 → 20 = 10I₁ + 12 → I₁ = 0.8 A, I₂ = 2.8 A. The 6 Ω carries I₂ = 2.8 A.

questions.questionText: A 12 V source (positive terminal up) feeds the top node T through 2 Ω. A 4 Ω resistor joins T to the bottom rail, and a second 4 Ω resistor joins T to the positive terminal of a 6 V source whose negative terminal is on the bottom rail. The current in the middle 4 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: Nodal at T: (12 − V)/2 = V/4 + (V − 6)/4 → 6 + 1.5 = V(0.5 + 0.25 + 0.25) → V = 7.5 V. Current = 7.5/4 = 1.875 A. Reversing the 6 V source gives 1.125 A; ignoring it gives 1.5 A.

questions.questionText: For the same circuit (12 V behind 2 Ω feeding node T, 4 Ω from T to the bottom rail, 4 Ω from T to a 6 V source), the power delivered by the 12 V source is:
questions.explanation: V_T = 7.5 V, so the 12 V source current is (12 − 7.5)/2 = 2.25 A and P = 12 × 2.25 = 27 W. Using the middle-branch current (1.875 A) gives the wrong 22.5 W.

questions.questionText: A 12 V source feeds node A through 4 Ω. A 6 Ω resistor from A to the reference carries current I_x. A current-controlled current source of value 0.5 I_x also injects current into node A. The voltage of node A is:
questions.explanation: KCL at A with I_x = V/6: (12 − V)/4 + 0.5(V/6) = V/6 → 3 = V(1/4 + 1/12) = V/3 → V = 9 V. Ignoring the dependent source gives 7.2 V; reversing it gives 6 V.

questions.questionText: A 10 V source is connected across A (+) and B. The bridge arms are AC = 2 Ω, CB = 3 Ω, AD = 4 Ω and DB = 1 Ω, and a 5 Ω galvanometer is connected between C and D. Using nodal or mesh analysis, the galvanometer current is:
questions.explanation: The bridge is unbalanced (2/3 ≠ 4/1). Nodal with B as reference: at C, (10 − V_C)/2 = V_C/3 + (V_C − V_D)/5; at D, (10 − V_D)/4 + (V_C − V_D)/5 = V_D/1. Solving gives V_C = 5.314 V, V_D = 2.457 V, so I = 2.857/5 = 0.571 A from C to D.

questions.questionText: Three practical sources are connected in parallel across a 4 Ω load: 12 V with 2 Ω, 6 V with 3 Ω, and 3 V with 6 Ω, the last one connected with reversed polarity. Using source transformation, the load current is:
questions.explanation: Currents: 12/2 = 6 A, 6/3 = 2 A, −3/6 = −0.5 A → 7.5 A. Total conductance = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 + 1/4 = 1.25 S, so V = 7.5/1.25 = 6 V and I_L = 6/4 = 1.5 A. Ignoring the reversal gives 8.5/1.25/4 = 1.7 A; the answer 6 A is the load voltage mistaken for current.

questions.questionText: A ladder network has a source V_s in series with 4 Ω feeding node A; A has a 12 Ω resistor to the reference and a 2 Ω resistor to node B; B has a 4 Ω load to the reference. What source voltage gives exactly 1 A in the load?
questions.explanation: Work back with KVL and KCL: V_B = 1 × 4 = 4 V; V_A = 4 + 1 × 2 = 6 V; I_12Ω = 6/12 = 0.5 A; source current = 1.5 A; V_s = 6 + 1.5 × 4 = 12 V.

questions.questionText: A single loop contains a 20 V independent source, resistors of 2 Ω and 3 Ω, and a current-controlled voltage source of value 5I (I = loop current) whose polarity opposes the current, like a drop. The loop current and the power absorbed by the dependent source are:
questions.explanation: KVL: 20 = 2I + 3I + 5I → I = 2 A. The dependent source drops 5 × 2 = 10 V with current entering its + terminal, so it absorbs 10 × 2 = 20 W. Ignoring it gives 20/5 = 4 A.

subtopics.title: Superposition Theorem
subtopics.subtitle: Solve multi-source linear circuits one independent source at a time

concepts.text: Statement

In a linear circuit containing more than one independent source, the response at any element (the voltage across it or the current through it) equals the algebraic sum of the responses produced by each independent source acting alone, with all other independent sources deactivated. Linearity means additivity (the response to a sum of inputs is the sum of the responses) and homogeneity (scaling the input scales the response). Resistors, inductors and capacitors are linear; diodes and transistors are not, so the theorem applies to linear circuits only.
Deactivating a Source

rows: Its voltage is forced to zero; any current may pass
Its current is forced to zero; any voltage may appear
Only the ideal part is switched off
Its value is set by circuit variables, not by an input

concepts.text: Procedure
Step by step:
items: 1. Select one independent source. Replace every other independent voltage source by a short circuit and every other independent current source by an open circuit. Leave dependent sources and all passive elements untouched.
2. Solve the resulting single-source circuit by series-parallel reduction, Ohm's law or the divider rules, and record the direction (or polarity) of the response.
3. Repeat for each remaining independent source.
4. Add the partial responses algebraically: contributions in the same direction add, contributions in opposite directions subtract.

concepts.text: Why Power Cannot Be Superposed

Power is a quadratic quantity (P = I²R = V²/R), so it is not a linear response. If two sources produce currents I₁ and I₂ in the same resistor, the true power is (I₁ + I₂)²R, which contains the cross term 2I₁I₂R that is absent from I₁²R + I₂²R. Always superpose currents or voltages first and compute power from the total.

concepts.plainText: (I1 + I2)² R ≠ I1² R + I2² R

concepts.text: Worked Example

A 12 V source with a 4 Ω series resistor is connected across a 6 Ω resistor. A 3 A current source is also connected directly across the 6 Ω resistor and pushes current through it in the same direction as the 12 V source does. Find the current in the 6 Ω resistor and the power it dissipates.
Solution by superposition:
items: 12 V source alone (open the current source): 4 Ω and 6 Ω are in series, so I' = 12/(4 + 6) = 1.2 A through the 6 Ω.

3 A source alone (short the voltage source): the 4 Ω now sits in parallel with the 6 Ω across the current source; by current division I'' = 3 × 4/(4 + 6) = 1.2 A through the 6 Ω, in the same direction.
Total current: I = 1.2 + 1.2 = 2.4 A.
Power: P = 2.4² × 6 = 34.56 W. Adding the partial powers (1.2² × 6 + 1.2² × 6 = 17.28 W) would give exactly half the true value; the missing cross term is 2 × 1.2 × 1.2 × 6 = 17.28 W.

concepts.text: The same method works for AC circuits with phasors, and it is the only elementary way to handle sources of different frequencies: solve for each frequency separately and add the time-domain responses.
Going Deeper: Superposition

Why superposition works: nodal or mesh analysis of a linear circuit gives a set of linear equations [G][V] = [I_s] whose right-hand side contains only the independent sources. The solution is [V] = [G]⁻¹[I_s], so every node voltage, and hence every branch current, is a weighted sum of the source values. Each weight is the response to that source alone with the others set to zero, which is exactly what superposition computes one source at a time.

concepts.latex: y = k_1 x_1 + k_2 x_2 + \cdots + k_n x_n
concepts.plainText: y = k1·x1 + k2·x2 + ... + kn·xn (response as weighted sum of independent sources)

concepts.text: The weights k are fixed by the passive elements and dependent sources only, so measuring the response twice with known source values lets you find them and predict the response for any other values. Dependent sources change the weights but do not add terms, which is why they stay in the circuit in every step.

Worked example 1: two voltage sources feeding one node
30 V behind 6 Ω and 12 V behind 3 Ω feed node T; T to ref 6 Ω.
30 V alone (12 V shorted): 3 ∥ 6 = 2 Ω
   V_T' = 30 × 2/(6 + 2) = 7.5 V  → I' in 6 Ω = 1.25 A
12 V alone (30 V shorted): 6 ∥ 6 = 3 Ω
   V_T'' = 12 × 3/(3 + 3) = 6 V   → I'' = 1 A
Total: V_T = 13.5 V, I = 2.25 A, P = 2.25² × 6 = 30.375 W
Nodal check: (5 + 4)/(1/6 + 1/3 + 1/6) = 9/0.6667 = 13.5 V  ✓
Wrong: I'²R + I''²R = 9.375 + 6 = 15.375 W

Worked example 2: dependent source kept active
20 V behind 5 Ω feeds node A; A to ref 10 Ω;
3 A independent source into A; dependent source draws 0.1·V_A out of A.
Node conductance with dependent source: 0.2 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.4 S
20 V alone: V' = (20/5)/0.4 = 10 V
3 A alone:  V'' = 3/0.4 = 7.5 V
V_A = 17.5 V
Check KCL: (20 − 17.5)/5 + 3 = 3.5 A in;
           17.5/10 + 0.1 × 17.5 = 1.75 + 1.75 = 3.5 A out  ✓

rows: A phasor exists for one frequency only
Cross terms average to zero over a period
Circuit with a diode or lamp

concepts.text: Sources of different frequencies are a special case worth remembering. If a resistor carries a DC current I₀ and sinusoids of RMS values I₁, I₂ at other frequencies, the products of different frequencies average to zero, so the average power is (I₀² + I₁² + I₂²)R and the RMS current is the square root of the sum of squares. A series capacitor passes none of the DC part in steady state, and an inductor offers no opposition to it.

concepts.plainText: I_rms = √(I0² + I1² + I2² + ...) for components of different frequencies

concepts.text: Common mistakes:
items: Opening a voltage source or shorting a current source instead of the reverse.
Removing the internal resistance of a practical source together with its EMF.
Switching off dependent sources.
Losing track of direction: record the direction of every partial current before adding.
Adding partial powers, or adding RMS magnitudes of same-frequency phasors that are out of phase.

concepts.text: Superposition is quickest when you need the contribution of one particular source, or when each single-source circuit collapses to a simple divider. For the full solution of a many-source circuit, nodal analysis is usually shorter; use it to check your superposition answer.

formulas.plainText: I = I' + I'' + I''' + ... (one term per independent source)
P = (I' + I'')² R, not I'² R + I''² R
Current divider: I1 = I × R2 / (R1 + R2)

notes.text: Superposition works for voltage and current but NOT directly for power. Power is nonlinear (I²R): add the partial currents first, then square.
Deactivating a source means setting its value to zero: voltage source → 0 V (short), current source → 0 A (open). Never remove the internal resistance of a practical source; it stays in the circuit.
Dependent (controlled) sources are never switched off. Treat them as ordinary circuit elements in every partial solution; only independent sources are taken one at a time.

formulas.title: Superposition of responses
formulas.description: Total current (or voltage) in an element is the algebraic sum of the partial responses, each found with only one independent source active.

formulas.title: Power from superposed current
formulas.description: Compute power only after adding the partial currents; the individual powers I'²R and I''²R do not add up to the true power.

formulas.title: Current divider
formulas.description: Current in R1 when a total current I splits between parallel R1 and R2; used in each single-source step.

flashcards.front: How is an independent current source deactivated when applying superposition?
flashcards.back: Replace it with an open circuit (0 A). An independent voltage source is replaced by a short circuit (0 V).

flashcards.front: Can superposition be used to find power directly?
flashcards.back: No. Power is proportional to I² or V², so add the partial currents or voltages first and then compute the power from the total.

flashcards.front: What happens to dependent sources during superposition?
flashcards.back: They stay active in every step. Only independent sources are switched on one at a time.

questions.questionText: In a linear circuit a 6 Ω resistor carries 2 A when one source acts alone and 0.5 A in the opposite direction when a second source acts alone. The actual current in the resistor and the power it dissipates are:
questions.explanation: Opposite directions subtract: I = 2 − 0.5 = 1.5 A. Power must be found from the total current, P = 1.5² × 6 = 13.5 W; adding the individual powers (24 W + 1.5 W = 25.5 W) is the superposition-of-power trap.

questions.questionText: While applying the superposition theorem to a circuit that contains a dependent source, the dependent source is:
options: Left active in the circuit during every step
questions.explanation: Only independent sources are considered one at a time. A dependent source's value is fixed by circuit voltages or currents, so it must remain in the circuit in every partial calculation.

questions.questionText: The superposition theorem is a direct consequence of which two properties of a linear circuit?
questions.explanation: Linearity means additivity (the response to x₁ + x₂ is y₁ + y₂) and homogeneity (the response to kx is ky). Superposition is additivity applied to the independent sources.

questions.questionText: When the superposition theorem is applied, an independent current source that is not being considered is replaced by:
options: A resistor equal to the load
A voltage source of equal value
questions.explanation: Deactivating a current source means setting its current to zero, which is an open circuit; its terminal voltage can still take any value.

questions.questionText: A practical voltage source of 24 V with an internal resistance of 0.5 Ω is to be deactivated in a superposition step. It is replaced by:
questions.explanation: Only the ideal EMF is set to zero (short circuit); the internal resistance is part of the circuit and must remain, so the source becomes a 0.5 Ω resistor.

questions.questionText: A linear circuit contains two independent voltage sources, one independent current source and one current-controlled voltage source. How many single-source circuits must be solved when superposition is applied one source at a time?
questions.explanation: Only independent sources are taken one at a time: 2 + 1 = 3 partial circuits. The dependent source stays active in each of them.

questions.questionText: During each step of the superposition method, the resistors, inductors and capacitors of the circuit are:
options: Removed along with the inactive sources
questions.explanation: Only the independent sources are switched on and off; every passive element stays exactly where it is.

questions.questionText: Source 1 acting alone produces +4 V across a resistor, and source 2 acting alone produces 1.5 V across the same resistor with the opposite polarity. The actual voltage across the resistor is:
questions.explanation: Opposite polarities subtract: V = 4 + (−1.5) = 2.5 V, with the polarity set by source 1.

questions.questionText: In a linear circuit, a 10 V source acting alone drives 1.5 A through a certain resistor. If that source is raised to 25 V (other sources still off), the current through the resistor due to it becomes:
questions.explanation: Homogeneity: the response scales with the source, so I = 1.5 × 25/10 = 3.75 A.

questions.questionText: The superposition theorem cannot be used directly to find which of these quantities?
options: The power dissipated in a resistor
questions.explanation: Currents and voltages are linear responses and can be added; power depends on I² or V², so it must be calculated from the total current or voltage.

questions.questionText: Two ideal voltage sources of 10 V and 6 V act in the same direction round a single loop containing an 8 Ω resistor. Using superposition, the loop current is:
questions.explanation: 10 V alone gives 10/8 = 1.25 A and 6 V alone gives 6/8 = 0.75 A in the same direction; total 2 A.

questions.questionText: A circuit is excited by a 50 Hz source and a 150 Hz source. The partial responses obtained by superposition must be added:
questions.explanation: A phasor is defined only for one frequency, so each frequency is solved separately and the results, such as 3 sin(ωt) and 2 sin(3ωt − 30°), are added in the time domain.

questions.questionText: Two ideal current sources of 3 A and 1 A both drive current in the same direction into a single 5 Ω resistor connected across them. By superposition, the voltage across the resistor is:
questions.explanation: 3 A alone gives 3 × 5 = 15 V and 1 A alone gives 1 × 5 = 5 V; the total is 20 V.

questions.questionText: With the voltage source shorted, a 3 A current source feeds a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor that are in parallel. The partial current in the 8 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: Current divider: I₈ = 3 × 4/(4 + 8) = 1 A. Using 8/(4 + 8) gives the 2 A that flows in the 4 Ω.

questions.questionText: With the current source opened, a 20 V source drives a 4 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor in series. The partial voltage across the 6 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: Voltage divider: V₆ = 20 × 6/(4 + 6) = 12 V; the 8 V appears across the 4 Ω.

questions.questionText: Every independent source in a linear resistive circuit is multiplied by 3. The power dissipated in any resistor becomes:
questions.explanation: By homogeneity every current is multiplied by 3, and since P = I²R the power grows by 3² = 9.

questions.questionText: A 24 V source in series with 4 Ω and a 12 V source in series with 4 Ω both feed node T (positive terminals toward T, negative terminals on the reference). A 2 Ω resistor joins T to the reference. The current in the 2 Ω resistor due to the 24 V source alone is:
questions.explanation: Short the 12 V source: 4 Ω ∥ 2 Ω = 1.333 Ω, source current = 24/(4 + 1.333) = 4.5 A, and the 2 Ω takes 4.5 × 4/6 = 3 A. The 4.5 A is the total source current, not the 2 Ω share.

questions.questionText: For the same circuit (24 V behind 4 Ω and 12 V behind 4 Ω feeding node T, 2 Ω from T to the reference), the total current in the 2 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: 24 V alone gives 3 A; 12 V alone gives [12/(4 + 1.333)] × 4/6 = 1.5 A in the same direction; total 4.5 A. Check by nodal: V_T = (6 + 3)/(0.25 + 0.25 + 0.5) = 9 V, and 9/2 = 4.5 A.

questions.questionText: An 18 V source in series with 3 Ω is connected across a 6 Ω resistor. A 3 A current source is also connected across the 6 Ω resistor, driving current through it in the direction opposite to that driven by the 18 V source. The current in the 6 Ω resistor is:
options: 3 A in the direction set by the 18 V source
2 A in the direction set by the 18 V source
1 A in the direction set by the 18 V source
1 A in the direction set by the current source
questions.explanation: 18 V alone: 18/(3 + 6) = 2 A. 3 A alone: 3 × 3/(3 + 6) = 1 A in the opposite direction. Net 2 − 1 = 1 A in the direction of the 18 V source's contribution.

questions.questionText: A 4 A current source feeds node A and a 2 A current source feeds node B, both from the reference. Resistors: A to reference 6 Ω, A to B 3 Ω, B to reference 3 Ω. By superposition, the voltage of node B is:
Two sources acting separately drive 1 A and 2 A, in the same direction, through a 5 Ω resistor. By how much does the sum of the two individual powers fall short of the true power in the resistor?
questions.explanation: True P = (1 + 2)² × 5 = 45 W; individual powers 1² × 5 + 2² × 5 = 25 W. The shortfall is the cross term 2 × 1 × 2 × 5 = 20 W.

questions.questionText: Which statement about deactivated sources in a superposition step is correct?
options: A shorted voltage source carries no current
An opened current source always has zero voltage across it
Deactivated sources are removed together with their internal resistances
A shorted voltage source may carry current, and an opened current source may have a voltage across it
questions.explanation: A short fixes only the voltage (0 V) and an open fixes only the current (0 A); the other variable is set by the rest of the circuit.

questions.questionText: Two sources of the same frequency produce phasor currents of 5∠0° A and 5∠60° A (RMS) in the same resistor. The RMS current in the resistor is:
questions.explanation: Superpose the phasors: 5 + (2.5 + j4.33) = 7.5 + j4.33, magnitude √(7.5² + 4.33²) = 8.66 A. Adding magnitudes gives 10 A, which is correct only if the currents are in phase.

questions.questionText: A 10 Ω resistor carries a 3 A DC current from one source and a 4 A RMS sinusoidal current from another source. The average power in the resistor is:
questions.explanation: For different frequencies the cross term averages to zero, so P = (3² + 4²) × 10 = 250 W, and the RMS current is 5 A. (3 + 4)² × 10 = 490 W wrongly adds the currents directly.

questions.questionText: In a linear circuit with sources V₁ and V₂, V₁ = 10 V acting alone gives 2 A through a resistor, and V₂ = 5 V acting alone gives 0.5 A through it in the opposite direction. What current flows when V₁ = 15 V and V₂ = 20 V act together?
Which of the following statements about the superposition theorem is NOT correct?
options: It applies to linear circuits with more than one independent source
Dependent sources are deactivated in the same way as independent sources
Power must be calculated from the total current or voltage
It can be used in AC circuits with phasors of the same frequency
questions.explanation: Dependent sources depend on circuit variables and must stay active in every partial circuit; switching them off gives wrong results. The other three statements are correct.

questions.questionText: A 30 V source in series with 5 Ω feeds node A. A 10 Ω resistor joins A to the reference, and a 2 A current source draws current out of node A to the reference. By superposition, the voltage of node A is:
A resistor is connected in series with an ideal current source. When that current source is deactivated during superposition, the resistor:
options: Is short-circuited along with the source
Carries no current, because the branch is open-circuited
Carries the same current as before
Must be replaced by an open circuit before the source is removed
questions.explanation: Opening the current source breaks the whole series branch, so the resistor carries zero current in that partial circuit. When the source is active the branch current equals the source current whatever the resistor's value.

questions.questionText: Three sources act on a 4 Ω resistor. Acting alone, the 12 V source drives 1.5 A through it from left to right, the 6 V source drives 0.5 A from right to left, and the 1 A current source drives 0.25 A from left to right. The resultant current is:
questions.explanation: Taking left to right as positive: I = 1.5 − 0.5 + 0.25 = 1.25 A, left to right.

questions.questionText: The main practical drawback of the superposition theorem compared with nodal or mesh analysis is that:
options: A separate circuit must be solved for each independent source
It works only for DC circuits
questions.explanation: Superposition is exact for linear circuits and handles any source type, but with many sources it means solving many circuits; it is most useful when each partial circuit reduces easily or when the contribution of one source is wanted.

questions.questionText: A 10 V source in series with 2 Ω feeds node A, and a 3 Ω resistor joins A to the reference. A current source is also connected between A and the reference. In the step where only the 10 V source acts, the voltage across the terminals of the opened current source is:
questions.explanation: With the current source open, 2 Ω and 3 Ω form a divider: V_A = 10 × 3/5 = 6 V. An opened current source has zero current, not zero voltage.

questions.questionText: Analysing a transistor amplifier separately for DC bias conditions and for the small AC signal, then combining the results, is justified by:
options: Superposition applied to the linearised small-signal model
Source transformation of the bias supply
questions.explanation: Around a fixed operating point the transistor is replaced by a linear model, so the DC (bias) response and the AC (signal) response can be found separately and added.

questions.questionText: Two 10 V sources, each in series with 5 Ω, feed node A with positive terminals toward A; a 5 Ω load joins A to the reference. By superposition, the voltage of node A is:

An ideal 12 V source is connected between node A and the reference, and a 6 Ω resistor is connected directly across it. Node A is joined to node B by 3 Ω; node B has 4 Ω to the reference and a 2 A current source feeding into it. The current in the 6 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: The 6 Ω is directly across the ideal 12 V source, so its current is 12/6 = 2 A whatever the rest of the circuit does. In superposition, the 2 A source contributes nothing to it because the shorted voltage source short-circuits the 6 Ω.

questions.questionText: A network has two sources: 10 V behind 2 Ω and 20 V behind 3 Ω, both connected in parallel across output terminals a–b with positive terminals at a. Using superposition, the open-circuit (Thevenin) voltage V_ab is:
questions.explanation: 10 V alone: 10 × 3/(2 + 3) = 6 V. 20 V alone: 20 × 2/(2 + 3) = 8 V. V_ab = 6 + 8 = 14 V. 6 V is only the first contribution.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the way sources are handled in superposition is correct?
options: Sources may be taken singly or in groups, in any order, and the final result is the same
Voltage sources must always be taken before current sources
Each source must be taken singly; grouping two sources is not allowed
The result depends on the order in which sources are taken
questions.explanation: Additivity holds for any split of the inputs, so sources can be taken one at a time or in convenient groups, in any order, and the partial results add to the same total.

questions.questionText: A two-source network gives 2 A in a resistor with source 1 alone and 3 A (same direction) with source 2 alone, but 4 A is measured with both sources active. The most likely conclusion is:
options: The network is linear and the result is expected
The two sources are dependent on each other
The network contains a non-linear element, so superposition does not hold
One of the partial measurements must have used a shorted current source
questions.explanation: For a linear network superposition predicts 2 + 3 = 5 A. A different measured value shows the response is not additive, which is the signature of a non-linear element (e.g. a diode or lamp).

questions.questionText: Superposition can NOT be applied directly to a resistive network that contains:
options: A tungsten lamp whose resistance rises with current
A dependent current source controlled by a resistor current
questions.explanation: A resistance that changes with current makes the V–I relation non-linear, violating additivity. Fixed R, L, C and linear dependent sources keep the circuit linear.

questions.questionText: A 5 A current source feeds node A, a 2 A current source draws current out of node A, and node A has 4 Ω and 12 Ω resistors to the reference. By superposition, the voltage of node A is:
questions.explanation: 4 Ω ∥ 12 Ω = 3 Ω. 5 A alone: +15 V; 2 A alone: −6 V; total 15 − 6 = 9 V.

questions.questionText: A 12 V source behind 2 Ω and a second source V₂ behind 3 Ω both feed node T; a 6 Ω resistor joins T to the reference. For zero current in the 6 Ω resistor, V₂ must be:
options: 12 V connected with polarity opposite to the 12 V source
8 V connected with polarity opposite to the 12 V source
18 V connected with the same polarity as the 12 V source
18 V connected with polarity opposite to the 12 V source
questions.explanation: Zero current means V_T = 0, so the 2 Ω carries 12/2 = 6 A and the 3 Ω must carry 6 A back: |V₂| = 6 × 3 = 18 V, opposing. By superposition the two partial currents in 6 Ω, (12/2)k and (V₂/3)k, must cancel.

questions.questionText: A 10 V DC source and a 10 V (RMS) 50 Hz AC source are connected in series and drive a series combination of R = 10 Ω and a capacitor with X_C = 10 Ω at 50 Hz. In steady state, the RMS current is:
questions.explanation: DC alone: the capacitor blocks steady DC, so I_dc = 0. AC alone: |Z| = √(10² + 10²) = 14.14 Ω, I = 10/14.14 = 0.707 A. Total RMS = √(0² + 0.707²) = 0.707 A. 1.225 A wrongly lets 1 A DC flow.

questions.questionText: In the circuit with a 24 V source behind 4 Ω and a 12 V source behind 4 Ω feeding node T, and 2 Ω from T to the reference, the 12 V source is reversed. The new current in the 2 Ω resistor and its power are:
questions.explanation: Contributions: 3 A from the 24 V source and 1.5 A from the 12 V source, now opposing: I = 3 − 1.5 = 1.5 A. P = 1.5² × 2 = 4.5 W. Subtracting partial powers (18 − 4.5) or adding them gives wrong values.

questions.questionText: A 10 V source in series with 2 Ω feeds node A; a 3 Ω resistor joins A to the reference, and a 5 A current source feeds node A from the reference. Using superposition, find the current in the 10 V source and whether it delivers or absorbs power.
options: 1 A into its + terminal; it absorbs 10 W
2 A out of its + terminal; it delivers 20 W
3 A into its + terminal; it absorbs 30 W
1 A out of its + terminal; it delivers 10 W
questions.explanation: 10 V alone: 10/(2 + 3) = 2 A out of the + terminal. 5 A alone (source shorted): the 2 Ω takes 5 × 3/5 = 3 A, flowing into the + terminal. Net 3 − 2 = 1 A into the + terminal, so the source absorbs 10 × 1 = 10 W.

questions.questionText: A 10 V source behind 2 Ω feeds node A; node A has a 4 Ω resistor to the reference, a 2 A independent current source feeding into it, and a dependent current source that draws 0.25·V_A amperes out of A to the reference. Using superposition, V_A is:
questions.explanation: Keep the dependent source active in both steps; the node conductance is 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 1 S. 10 V alone: V' = 5/1 = 5 V; 2 A alone: V'' = 2/1 = 2 V; V_A = 7 V. Wrongly switching off the dependent source gives 6.67 + 2.67 = 9.33 V.

questions.questionText: In a linear circuit, with V₁ = 10 V and V₂ = 10 V a resistor current of 4 A is measured; with V₁ = 10 V and V₂ reversed to −10 V the current is 1 A. What current flows when V₁ = 20 V and V₂ = 5 V?

Node A is fed by a 12 V source behind 3 Ω, a 6 V source behind 6 Ω (positive terminals toward A) and a 1 A current source; a 2 Ω load joins A to the reference. The load current due to the 6 V source alone, and the total load current, are:
questions.explanation: With the other sources off, A sees 3 ∥ 6 ∥ 2 = 1 Ω. 6 V alone: (6/6) × 1 = 1 V → 0.5 A. 12 V alone: (12/3) × 1 = 4 V → 2 A. 1 A alone: 1 V → 0.5 A. Total 2 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 3 A.

questions.questionText: A 30 V source behind 6 Ω feeds node A; A has 3 Ω to the reference and 2 Ω to node B; B has 6 Ω to the reference and a 4 A current source feeding into it. By superposition, the voltage of node A is:

A single loop contains two independent sources, 12 V and 6 V, aiding each other, resistors of 2 Ω and 4 Ω, and a current-controlled voltage source of 3I (I = loop current) that acts as a drop. By superposition, the power delivered by the 12 V source is:
questions.explanation: Keep the dependent source in both steps, so the loop behaves as 2 + 4 + 3 = 9 Ω. 12 V alone: 1.333 A; 6 V alone: 0.667 A; I = 2 A. P = 12 × 2 = 24 W. Switching the dependent source off gives I = 3 A and 36 W; using only the 12 V contribution gives 16 W.

subtopics.title: Thevenin's Theorem
subtopics.subtitle: Reduce any linear two-terminal network to V_th in series with R_th

concepts.text: Statement

Any linear, bilateral two-terminal network containing sources and resistances can be replaced, as seen from those two terminals A-B, by a single voltage source V_th in series with a single resistance R_th. A load connected between A and B cannot tell the difference: it receives the same voltage and the same current from the equivalent as from the original network. The theorem is most useful when one element (the load) is changed repeatedly while the rest of the circuit stays fixed.
Thevenin Voltage V_th

V_th is the open-circuit voltage across terminals A-B: remove the load, keep every source active and find the voltage between A and B by any method (voltage division, nodal analysis, superposition). Because nothing is connected across the terminals, no current leaves them, which is why V_th is also written V_oc.
Thevenin Resistance R_th
Three ways to find R_th:
items: Kill the sources: remove the load, replace independent voltage sources by short circuits and independent current sources by open circuits, then compute the resistance seen looking into A-B.
Ratio method: R_th = V_oc/I_sc, where I_sc is the current through a short circuit placed across A-B. This is the method to use when dependent sources are present.
Test-source method: with the independent sources killed, apply a 1 V (or 1 A) test source at A-B and take R_th = V_test/I_test.

concepts.plainText: R_th = V_oc / I_sc

concepts.text: Procedure
Solving a load problem with Thevenin's theorem:
items: 1. Identify the load element, remove it and mark the terminals A-B.
2. Find V_th = V_oc across A-B with all sources active.
3. Find R_th by killing the sources (or from V_oc/I_sc).
4. Draw V_th in series with R_th and reconnect the load R_L.
5. Load current I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L); load voltage V_L = V_th × R_L/(R_th + R_L).

concepts.plainText: I_L = V_th / (R_th + R_L)

concepts.text: Worked Example
A 24 V source feeds a series string of 4 Ω and 12 Ω. A load R_L = 6 Ω is connected across the 12 Ω resistor. Find the load current using Thevenin's theorem.
Solution:
items: Remove R_L. By voltage division the open-circuit voltage across the 12 Ω is V_th = 24 × 12/(4 + 12) = 18 V.
Kill the source (replace it by a short). Looking into the terminals, the 4 Ω and 12 Ω are in parallel: R_th = (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3 Ω.
Reconnect R_L: I_L = 18/(3 + 6) = 2 A and V_L = 2 × 6 = 12 V.
Check against the original circuit: 12 Ω in parallel with 6 Ω is 4 Ω, total current 24/(4 + 4) = 3 A, voltage across the parallel pair 3 × 4 = 12 V, so I_L = 12/6 = 2 A, the same answer.

concepts.text: Relation to Norton

Thevenin and Norton equivalents are source transformations of each other: I_N = V_th/R_th, R_N = R_th and V_th = I_N R_N. Both describe the same terminal behaviour; choose Thevenin when the load is in series with the source path and Norton when parallel branches dominate.
Going Deeper: Thevenin's Theorem

Why can a whole network be squeezed into just two numbers? For a linear network the relation between the terminal voltage V and the current I drawn from the terminals is a straight line. A straight line is fixed by two points: its intercept on the voltage axis (I = 0, the open-circuit voltage) and its intercept on the current axis (V = 0, the short-circuit current). A voltage source V_th in series with R_th has exactly the same straight line, so it is indistinguishable from the original network at those terminals.

concepts.plainText: V = V_th − R_th × I (terminal line of any linear two-terminal network)

concepts.text: The formal proof uses superposition. Drive the terminals with a test current source I and split the response into two parts: the voltage with all internal sources active and I = 0, which is V_oc, and the voltage due to I alone with the internal independent sources killed, which is −R_th I. Adding the two gives V = V_oc − R_th I. This is also why the theorem needs the network to be linear, while the load attached to the equivalent may be anything, even a diode.
Special cases worth recognising at a glance:
items: A resistor connected directly across an ideal voltage source does not affect V_th or R_th and can be deleted.
A resistor in series with an ideal current source does not affect V_th or R_th either; the source forces its current regardless.
A network with only resistors and dependent sources has V_th = 0; only R_th exists and it must be found with a test source.
A balanced Wheatstone bridge gives V_th = 0 across the detector terminals, so no detector current flows whatever its resistance.
An ideal current source on its own has no Thevenin equivalent (R_th would be infinite), just as an ideal voltage source has no Norton equivalent.

concepts.text:
Example 1: 12 V source with 3 Ω to node A, a 2 A source injecting into A,
6 Ω from A to B (source negative). Find the current in a 4 Ω load across A-B.
V_th (nodal at A, load removed): (12 − V)/3 + 2 = V/6
  4 − V/3 + 2 = V/6  ->  6 = V/2  ->  V_th = 12 V
R_th: short the 12 V source, open the 2 A source: 3 Ω || 6 Ω = 2 Ω
I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L) = 12/(2 + 4) = 2 A

Example 2 (dependent source): 18 V source in series with 6 Ω to node A;
a VCCS draws (1/3)·V_A amperes from A to B. Load R_L = 4 Ω.
V_oc: (18 − V)/6 = V/3  ->  3 = V/6 + V/3 = V/2  ->  V_oc = 6 V
I_sc: V_A = 0, so the VCCS carries 0 A; I_sc = 18/6 = 3 A
R_th = V_oc/I_sc = 6/3 = 2 Ω   (killing the VCCS would wrongly give 6 Ω)
I_L = 6/(2 + 4) = 1 A

Example 3 (from two load tests): a 3 Ω load draws 2 A, an 8 Ω load draws 1 A.
V_th = I(R_th + R_L) for both tests:
  2(R_th + 3) = 1(R_th + 8)  ->  2R_th + 6 = R_th + 8  ->  R_th = 2 Ω
  V_th = 2 × (2 + 3) = 10 V
Check: 10/(2 + 8) = 1 A

rows: Solve the network twice (open, then shorted)
Dependent sources, or I_sc is easy
Kill independent sources, apply 1 V or 1 A
Measure V and I for two different loads

concepts.text: The theorem carries straight over to sinusoidal steady state: V_th becomes a phasor open-circuit voltage and R_th becomes the complex impedance Z_th seen from the terminals, found with the same rules. The load current is then V_th/(Z_th + Z_L), computed with complex arithmetic; adding impedance magnitudes instead of complex values is a common error.
Common mistakes:
items: Leaving the load connected while finding V_th or R_th.
Killing a dependent source; dependent sources always stay in the circuit.
Shorting a current source (or opening a voltage source) when killing sources.
Assuming the power lost in R_th equals the power lost inside the original network; the equivalence holds only at the terminals.

concepts.text: For ladder networks, apply Thevenin step by step from the source end: convert the source and first shunt resistor to a Thevenin equivalent, add the next series resistor, repeat. Each step is a one-line divider calculation.

formulas.plainText: I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L); V_L = V_th R_L/(R_th + R_L)

formulas.latex: V_{th} = V_s \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}, \qquad R_{th} = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}
formulas.plainText: For a divider: V_th = V_s R2/(R1 + R2); R_th = R1 R2/(R1 + R2)

notes.text: To find R_th: kill all sources (short voltage sources, open current sources) and find the resistance seen from the terminals. Remove the load first; it is never part of R_th.
Never kill a dependent source. When one is present, find R_th from V_oc/I_sc or with a test source; killing only the independent sources and 'looking in' gives the wrong answer.
A resistor connected directly across an ideal voltage source has no effect on V_th or R_th (it is shorted when the source is killed and does not change the source voltage), so it can be ignored.

formulas.title: Thevenin voltage
formulas.description: The open-circuit voltage across the load terminals with the load removed and every source active.

formulas.title: Thevenin resistance
formulas.description: Ratio of open-circuit voltage to short-circuit current at the terminals; equals the dead-network resistance when only independent sources are present.

formulas.title: Load current from Thevenin equivalent
formulas.description: Current in any load R_L connected to the equivalent; recompute only this line when the load changes.

formulas.title: Load voltage from Thevenin equivalent
formulas.description: Voltage across the load by voltage division between R_th and R_L.

flashcards.front: How is the Thevenin voltage V_th defined?
flashcards.back: It is the open-circuit voltage across the two load terminals after the load is removed, with every source still active.

flashcards.front: A network gives V_oc = 10 V and I_sc = 2 A. What is its Thevenin equivalent?
flashcards.back: V_th = 10 V in series with R_th = 10/2 = 5 Ω.

flashcards.front: Why does Thevenin's theorem save work when the load changes?
flashcards.back: V_th and R_th are found once; each new load needs only I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L) instead of re-solving the whole network.

questions.questionText: A 30 V source drives a 10 Ω and a 20 Ω resistor connected in series. With respect to the two terminals of the 20 Ω resistor, the Thevenin equivalent of the network is:
questions.explanation: V_th is the open-circuit voltage across the 20 Ω: 30 × 20/(10 + 20) = 20 V. Killing the source puts the 10 Ω and 20 Ω in parallel as seen from the terminals: R_th = (10 × 20)/30 = 6.67 Ω.

questions.questionText: The open-circuit voltage at the terminals of a linear network is 24 V and the short-circuit current is 6 A. The Thevenin resistance of the network is:
questions.explanation: R_th = V_oc/I_sc = 24/6 = 4 Ω. This ratio method works even when the network contains dependent sources.

questions.questionText: Thevenin's theorem can be used to replace part of a circuit by a voltage source and a series resistance only if that part is:
options: Free of resistors connected in parallel
Linear (made of linear elements and sources)
questions.explanation: The theorem rests on the straight-line V-I relation of a linear network. Current sources, parallel resistors and AC sources are all allowed; nonlinearity is what breaks it.

questions.questionText: While finding the Thevenin resistance of a network, an ideal independent current source is replaced by:
options: An ideal voltage source of equal value
questions.explanation: Killing a current source means setting its current to zero, which is an open circuit (infinite internal resistance).

questions.questionText: A Thevenin equivalent of 12 V in series with 2 Ω supplies a 4 Ω load. The load current is:
questions.explanation: I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L) = 12/(2 + 4) = 2 A. Using only R_th (6 A) or only R_L (3 A) is a common slip.

questions.questionText: A network has V_th = 10 V and R_th = 5 Ω. The voltage across a 20 Ω load connected to its terminals is:
questions.explanation: V_L = V_th × R_L/(R_th + R_L) = 10 × 20/25 = 8 V. The remaining 2 V is dropped across R_th.

questions.questionText: An ideal voltmeter across terminals A-B of a linear network reads 15 V and an ideal ammeter across the same terminals reads 3 A. When a 5 Ω resistor is connected across A-B, the current in it is:
questions.explanation: V_th = 15 V and R_th = V_oc/I_sc = 15/3 = 5 Ω, so I = 15/(5 + 5) = 1.5 A.

questions.questionText: Which statement about Thevenin's theorem is correct?
options: Both the network being replaced and the load must be linear
The Thevenin resistance depends on the value of the load resistance
The load connected to the equivalent may be nonlinear, but the network being replaced must be linear
The Thevenin voltage is measured with the load connected
questions.explanation: The equivalence concerns only the network behind the terminals, so any load, even a diode, can be analysed with it. R_th and V_th are found with the load removed and do not depend on it.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a Thevenin equivalent is NOT correct?
options: The power dissipated in R_th equals the power dissipated inside the original network
It gives the same load current as the original network for every load
It gives the same open-circuit voltage as the original network
It gives the same short-circuit current as the original network
questions.explanation: The equivalence holds only at the terminals. Internal power is generally different; for example, with the terminals open R_th dissipates nothing, while resistors inside the original network may still carry current.

questions.questionText: Before calculating the Thevenin voltage across terminals A-B, the load connected between A and B is:
questions.explanation: V_th is the open-circuit voltage, so the load is removed and no current leaves the terminals.

questions.questionText: An 18 V source is in series with 6 Ω. A 3 Ω resistor connects the far end of the 6 Ω to terminal B (the source's negative terminal), and a 4 Ω resistor runs from the junction of the 6 Ω and 3 Ω to terminal A. The Thevenin equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: No current flows in the 4 Ω with A-B open, so V_th = 18 × 3/(6 + 3) = 6 V. R_th = (6 || 3) + 4 = 2 + 4 = 6 Ω; forgetting the 4 Ω gives 2 Ω.

questions.questionText: An ideal 5 A current source is in parallel with a 4 Ω resistor. A 6 Ω resistor connects the top of this pair to terminal A; terminal B is the bottom of the pair. The Thevenin equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: With A-B open all 5 A flows in the 4 Ω, so V_th = 5 × 4 = 20 V (the 6 Ω carries no current). Opening the current source leaves 4 + 6 = 10 Ω in series; 2.4 Ω is the parallel mix-up.

questions.questionText: A 10 V source feeds two parallel arms. Arm 1 is 4 Ω (top) in series with 6 Ω (bottom); arm 2 is 6 Ω (top) in series with 4 Ω (bottom). A 5.2 Ω load is connected between the midpoints of the two arms. Using Thevenin's theorem, the load current is:
questions.explanation: Midpoint voltages are 10 × 6/10 = 6 V and 10 × 4/10 = 4 V, so V_th = 2 V. With the source shorted, R_th = (4 || 6) + (6 || 4) = 2.4 + 2.4 = 4.8 Ω. I = 2/(4.8 + 5.2) = 0.2 A.

questions.questionText: For a Wheatstone bridge in the balanced condition, the Thevenin voltage across the detector (galvanometer) terminals is:
options: Equal to the supply voltage divided by the Thevenin resistance
questions.explanation: At balance both midpoints are at the same potential, so V_th = 0 and no detector current flows whatever its resistance.

questions.questionText: A 20 V source in series with 5 Ω is connected to terminal A; terminal B is the source's negative terminal. A voltage-controlled current source connected between A and B draws 0.05·V_AB amperes from A to B (V_AB in volts). The Thevenin equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: Open circuit: (20 − V)/5 = 0.05V gives 4 = 0.25V, V_oc = 16 V. Short circuit: V_AB = 0 so the dependent source carries nothing and I_sc = 20/5 = 4 A. R_th = 16/4 = 4 Ω; killing the dependent source would wrongly give 5 Ω.

questions.questionText: Starting at terminal B, a 10 V source (positive terminal away from B) is followed by a 2 Ω resistor carrying current I towards terminal A, and then by a current-controlled voltage source whose voltage 4I (volts, I in amperes) drops in the direction of I, ending at A. The Thevenin equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: V_AB = 10 − 2I − 4I = 10 − 6I. Open circuit: I = 0, so V_oc = 10 V. Short circuit: 10 − 6I = 0, I_sc = 1.667 A, so R_th = 10/1.667 = 6 Ω. The dependent source behaves like an extra 4 Ω and must not be shorted.

questions.questionText: A two-terminal network contains only resistors and dependent sources, with no independent source. Its Thevenin equivalent is:
options: V_th = 0 with R_th found by applying a test source at the terminals
V_th equal to the dependent-source value with R_th = 0
Undefined, because the theorem needs an independent source
V_th = 0 with R_th found by killing the dependent sources
questions.explanation: Without an independent source nothing drives the network, so V_oc = 0. R_th still exists and is found by applying a 1 V or 1 A test source with the dependent sources left active.

questions.questionText: A 30 V source is in series with 10 Ω to node X. A 15 Ω resistor connects X to terminal B (the source's negative terminal), a 4 Ω resistor runs from X to terminal A, and a 6 Ω resistor connects A to B. The Thevenin equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: The 4 Ω + 6 Ω branch (10 Ω) is in parallel with 15 Ω, giving 6 Ω, so V_X = 30 × 6/16 = 11.25 V and V_th = 11.25 × 6/10 = 6.75 V. R_th = ((10 || 15) + 4) || 6 = 10 || 6 = 3.75 Ω. Ignoring the 6 Ω gives 18 V and 10 Ω.

questions.questionText: A network has V_th = 24 V and R_th = 4 Ω. The load resistance that will draw 2 A from it is:
questions.explanation: 2 = 24/(4 + R_L) gives 4 + R_L = 12, so R_L = 8 Ω. Taking 24/2 = 12 Ω forgets R_th.

questions.questionText: With a 2 Ω load across terminals A-B of a linear network the load voltage is 8 V; with a 6 Ω load it is 12 V. The Thevenin equivalent of the network is:
questions.explanation: Load currents are 8/2 = 4 A and 12/6 = 2 A. V_th = 8 + 4R_th = 12 + 2R_th gives R_th = 2 Ω and V_th = 16 V. Check: 16 × 6/8 = 12 V.

questions.questionText: The open-circuit voltage of a linear network is 20 V. When a 10 Ω load is connected, the terminal voltage falls to 16 V. The Thevenin resistance is:
questions.explanation: Load current = 16/10 = 1.6 A. The 4 V lost is dropped across R_th, so R_th = 4/1.6 = 2.5 Ω. Using 20/10 = 2 A for the current gives the wrong 2 Ω.

questions.questionText: The Thevenin resistance of an ideal voltage source is:
questions.explanation: An ideal voltage source keeps its voltage for any current, so its terminal line has zero slope: R_th = 0.

questions.questionText: For which of the following does a Thevenin equivalent NOT exist?
options: An ideal voltage source on its own
An ideal current source on its own
A voltage source in series with a resistor
questions.explanation: An ideal current source has infinite internal resistance and no finite open-circuit voltage, so it cannot be written as V_th in series with a finite R_th. A single resistor is simply V_th = 0 with R_th = R.

questions.questionText: Two branches are connected in parallel across terminals A-B: branch 1 is 12 V in series with 3 Ω, branch 2 is 6 V in series with 6 Ω, both sources having their positive terminals towards A. The Thevenin equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: Nodal at A: (12 − V)/3 + (6 − V)/6 = 0 gives 4 + 1 = V(1/3 + 1/6), V_th = 5/0.5 = 10 V. R_th = 3 || 6 = 2 Ω. Averaging the sources (9 V) ignores the unequal resistances.

questions.questionText: A 10 V source in series with 5 Ω is connected to node A with its positive side towards A; terminal B is its negative terminal. An ideal 2 A current source injects current into A from B. A 5 Ω load is connected across A-B. Using Thevenin's theorem, the load current is:
questions.explanation: With A-B open the 2 A must flow back through the 5 Ω into the source, so V_th = 10 + 2 × 5 = 20 V. R_th = 5 Ω (current source opened). I_L = 20/(5 + 5) = 2 A; ignoring the current source gives 1 A.

questions.questionText: The Thevenin resistance of a network containing only resistors and independent sources can be measured with an ohmmeter across A-B provided that:
options: The load is removed and every independent source is replaced by its internal resistance
The load is left connected and the sources remain active
Only the voltage sources are removed and current sources are left active
The terminals A-B are first short-circuited
questions.explanation: An ohmmeter measures resistance of a dead network. Voltage sources become shorts (plus any internal resistance), current sources become opens, and the load must be disconnected.

questions.questionText: When finding R_th, a practical voltage source of 9 V with internal resistance 0.5 Ω is replaced by:
options: A short circuit, ignoring the 0.5 Ω
questions.explanation: Only the ideal part of the source is killed (shorted); its internal resistance of 0.5 Ω remains in the network.

questions.questionText: An ideal 3 A current source in series with a 10 Ω resistor drives current into node A; a 5 Ω resistor connects A to terminal B, and the current source returns to B. The Thevenin equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: The ideal source forces 3 A through the 5 Ω whatever the series 10 Ω, so V_th = 3 × 5 = 15 V. Opening the current source leaves its series 10 Ω dangling, so R_th = 5 Ω.

questions.questionText: An ideal 12 V source has an 8 Ω resistor connected directly across its terminals. From its positive terminal a 4 Ω resistor runs to terminal A, and a 12 Ω resistor connects A to terminal B (the negative terminal). The Thevenin equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: The 8 Ω across the ideal source changes nothing at A-B. V_th = 12 × 12/(4 + 12) = 9 V and R_th = 4 || 12 = 3 Ω. Treating the 8 Ω as if it were in series gives 6 V and 6 Ω.

questions.questionText: A source of 50∠0° V (rms) is in series with an inductive reactance of j10 Ω, and a 10 Ω resistor is connected across terminals A-B at the far end. The Thevenin equivalent at A-B is:
options: 35.36∠45° V in series with (5 − j5) Ω
35.36∠−45° V in series with (5 + j5) Ω
50∠0° V in series with (10 + j10) Ω

questions.questionText: Thevenin's theorem is also known as the:
questions.explanation: Helmholtz stated the result in 1853 and Thevenin published it independently in 1883, hence the name Helmholtz–Thevenin theorem. Mayer–Norton is the current-source dual.

questions.questionText: A circuit has a Thevenin equivalent of 10 V in series with 10 kΩ. A voltmeter with an internal resistance of 90 kΩ is connected across its terminals. The voltmeter reads:
questions.explanation: The meter is a load: V = 10 × 90/(10 + 90) = 9 V. Only an ideal (infinite-resistance) voltmeter would read the full 10 V.

questions.questionText: A 24 V source, a 2 Ω resistor, a load R_L and a 4 Ω resistor are all connected in one series loop. With R_L removed, the Thevenin equivalent across the gap left by R_L is:
questions.explanation: With the loop open no current flows, so neither resistor drops any voltage and the full 24 V appears across the gap. Killing the source leaves 2 + 4 = 6 Ω in series.

questions.questionText: Every independent source in a linear resistive network is doubled in value. The Thevenin equivalent at a given pair of terminals becomes:
