options: V_th doubles and R_th is unchanged
V_th is unchanged and R_th halves
questions.explanation: V_th is a linear function of the sources, so it doubles. R_th is found with the sources killed and depends only on the resistances, so it does not change.

questions.questionText: A network has V_th = 18 V and R_th = 6 Ω. The current that flows if its terminals are short-circuited is:
questions.explanation: I_sc = V_th/R_th = 18/6 = 3 A.

questions.questionText: An ideal voltmeter reads 12 V across terminals A-B of a linear network. An ammeter with an internal resistance of 1 Ω connected across A-B reads 2 A. The Thevenin resistance of the network is:
questions.explanation: The ammeter is a 1 Ω load: 2 = 12/(R_th + 1), so R_th + 1 = 6 and R_th = 5 Ω. Treating the ammeter as ideal gives 6 Ω.

questions.questionText: As the load resistance connected to a fixed Thevenin equivalent is increased from zero towards infinity, the load voltage:
questions.explanation: V_L = V_th R_L/(R_th + R_L): zero for a short and approaching V_th as R_L becomes very large.

questions.questionText: Two identical batteries, each of 12 V emf and 0.5 Ω internal resistance, are connected in parallel (positive to positive). The Thevenin equivalent of the combination is:
questions.explanation: Equal emfs in parallel give V_th = 12 V; the internal resistances combine in parallel: 0.5 || 0.5 = 0.25 Ω. 24 V and 1 Ω are the series-connection values.

questions.questionText: An ideal 4 A current source is connected across terminals A-B together with a 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor, all three in parallel. The Thevenin voltage at A-B is:
questions.explanation: The resistors in parallel give 6 || 3 = 2 Ω, so V_th = 4 × 2 = 8 V. Multiplying by one resistor alone (24 V or 12 V) or by their sum (36 V) is wrong.

questions.questionText: A 40 V source is in series with 10 Ω to node X; a 10 Ω resistor connects X to the source's negative terminal B, and a 5 Ω resistor runs from X to terminal A. A 10 Ω load is connected across A-B. Using Thevenin's theorem step by step, the load current is:
questions.explanation: At X: V_th1 = 40 × 10/20 = 20 V and R_th1 = 10 || 10 = 5 Ω. Adding the 5 Ω gives 20 V in series with 10 Ω at A-B, so I_L = 20/(10 + 10) = 1 A.

questions.questionText: A network has V_th = 15 V and R_th = 3 Ω. The load resistance for which the load voltage is 12 V is:
questions.explanation: 12 = 15 R_L/(3 + R_L) gives 36 + 12R_L = 15R_L, so R_L = 12 Ω. Check: current 15/15 = 1 A, V_L = 12 V.

questions.questionText: A Thevenin equivalent of 20 V in series with 4 Ω supplies a 6 Ω load. The power delivered to the load is:
questions.explanation: I = 20/(4 + 6) = 2 A and P_L = I²R_L = 4 × 6 = 24 W. 16 W is the loss in R_th and 66.7 W wrongly uses V_th²/R_L.

questions.questionText: The correct way to find the Thevenin resistance of a network that contains dependent sources is to:
options: Kill all sources, dependent and independent, and combine the resistances
Replace each dependent source by the resistor that controls it
Apply a test source at the terminals (or use V_oc/I_sc) with the dependent sources left active
Declare R_th undefined, since dependent sources make the network nonlinear
questions.explanation: Dependent sources are part of the network's own behaviour and must stay active. A network with linear dependent sources is still linear, so R_th exists and is found by a test source or V_oc/I_sc.

questions.questionText: An ideal 6 A current source is in parallel with 2 Ω. A 3 Ω resistor connects the top of this pair to node A, a 5 Ω resistor connects A to the bottom of the pair (terminal B), and a 3.5 Ω load is connected across A-B. Using Thevenin's theorem, the load current is:
questions.explanation: 6 A || 2 Ω is 12 V in series with 2 Ω; adding 3 Ω gives 12 V with 5 Ω. With the 5 Ω shunt at A: V_th = 12 × 5/10 = 6 V and R_th = 5 || 5 = 2.5 Ω. I_L = 6/(2.5 + 3.5) = 1 A; ignoring the 5 Ω shunt gives 1.41 A.

questions.questionText: Thevenin's theorem saves the most work when:
options: The network contains only one resistor
The current in one element must be found for several different values of that element
Every element in the network is nonlinear
The load is an ideal voltage source
questions.explanation: V_th and R_th are found once; each new load value then needs only I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L).

questions.questionText: A Thevenin equivalent of 10∠0° V in series with Z_th = (3 + j4) Ω supplies a purely resistive 5 Ω load. The magnitude of the load current is:
questions.explanation: Z_total = 3 + j4 + 5 = 8 + j4 Ω with |Z| = √(64 + 16) = 8.94 Ω, so I = 10/8.94 = 1.12 A. Dropping j4 gives 1.25 A; adding magnitudes 5 + 5 gives 1.0 A.

questions.questionText: A Thevenin equivalent of 9 V in series with 3 Ω supplies a 3 Ω load. If the load is changed to 6 Ω, the load current:
questions.explanation: I = 9/(3 + 3) = 1.5 A before and 9/(3 + 6) = 1 A after. The current does not halve because R_th stays in the loop.

questions.questionText: In a network with two independent sources, the Thevenin voltage at a pair of terminals can be found by:
options: Adding the open-circuit voltages produced by each source acting alone
Adding the two source voltages directly
Taking the larger of the two source voltages
Multiplying one source's short-circuit current by the load resistance
questions.explanation: V_th is the open-circuit voltage of a linear network, so superposition applies: find V_oc with each source alone (the other killed) and add the results algebraically.

subtopics.title: Norton's Theorem
subtopics.subtitle: The current-source dual of Thevenin: I_N in parallel with R_N = R_th

concepts.text: Statement

Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced, as seen from its terminals A-B, by an equivalent circuit consisting of a single current source I_N in parallel with a single resistance R_N. Norton's theorem is the dual of Thevenin's: where Thevenin uses a voltage source with a series resistance, Norton uses a current source with a parallel resistance. Both equivalents give identical terminal behaviour for every possible load.
Norton Current I_N

I_N is the short-circuit current: replace the load by a short circuit (a zero-resistance wire) between A and B and calculate the current flowing through that short with all sources active. It is also written I_sc. Any element that ends up in parallel with the short carries no current and can be ignored in this step.
Norton Resistance R_N

R_N is exactly the Thevenin resistance: deactivate all independent sources (voltage sources → short circuit, current sources → open circuit), remove the load and find the resistance seen from A-B. Equivalently R_N = V_oc/I_sc, which must be used when dependent sources are present.

concepts.plainText: I_N = short-circuit current; R_N = R_th

concepts.text: Using the Equivalent
With a load R_L across the Norton equivalent, I_N divides between R_N and R_L:
items: Load current I_L = I_N × R_N/(R_N + R_L) (current-divider rule).
Load voltage V_L = I_L R_L = I_N × R_N R_L/(R_N + R_L).
A short-circuit load (R_L = 0) takes the whole I_N; an open-circuit load (R_L = ∞) develops V_oc = I_N R_N.

concepts.plainText: I_L = I_N × R_N / (R_N + R_L)

concepts.text: Thevenin-Norton Conversion

Converting one form to the other is a source transformation: V_th = I_N R_N and I_N = V_th/R_th, with the same resistance in both. The current-source arrow points toward the terminal that is positive in the Thevenin form. Because R_N = R_th, having either equivalent gives the other with one multiplication or division.
Worked Example

A 20 V source with a 5 Ω series resistor is connected to terminals A-B, across which a 20 Ω resistor is permanently connected as part of the network. A load R_L = 4 Ω is then attached to A-B. Find the load current using Norton's theorem.
Solution:
items: I_N: short A-B. The short bypasses the 20 Ω resistor, so I_sc = 20/5 = 4 A.
R_N: kill the source (short it) and look into A-B: 5 Ω in parallel with 20 Ω gives (5 × 20)/(5 + 20) = 4 Ω.
Norton equivalent: 4 A in parallel with 4 Ω. With R_L = 4 Ω: I_L = 4 × 4/(4 + 4) = 2 A and V_L = 2 × 4 = 8 V.
Cross-check via Thevenin: V_th = I_N R_N = 16 V (also 20 × 20/(5 + 20) = 16 V by voltage division), so I_L = 16/(4 + 4) = 2 A.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Norton's Theorem

Norton's theorem follows directly from Thevenin's. Rearranging the terminal line V = V_th − R_th I for the current gives I = V_th/R_th − V/R_th, which is exactly the equation of a current source I_N = V_th/R_th feeding the terminals with a resistance R_N = R_th connected in parallel. The two equivalents are therefore the same straight line on the V-I plane, read once from the voltage axis and once from the current axis.

concepts.plainText: I = I_N − V/R_N (terminal line in Norton form)

concepts.text: The Norton form is the natural choice when branches meet in parallel. Parallel Norton sources simply add their currents and their conductances, which is the basis of nodal analysis and Millman's theorem. It is also the standard model for devices that behave like current sources, such as the collector of a BJT or the drain of a MOSFET in saturation, modelled as a controlled current source in parallel with an output resistance r_o.

concepts.plainText: Parallel Norton sources: I_N = sum of I_k; 1/R_N = sum of 1/R_k

concepts.text:
Example 1: 36 V source with 6 Ω to node X, 12 Ω from X to B, 4 Ω from X to A.
I_N: short A-B. 4 || 12 = 3 Ω, total 6 + 3 = 9 Ω, source current 36/9 = 4 A
  current divider into the short: I_N = 4 × 12/(12 + 4) = 3 A
R_N: short the source: (6 || 12) + 4 = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω
Check: V_oc = 36 × 12/18 = 24 V = I_N R_N = 3 × 8 V
Load 8 Ω: I_L = 3 × 8/(8 + 8) = 1.5 A

Example 2: branch 1 = 10 V in series with 2 Ω, branch 2 = 3 A source || 4 Ω,
both across A-B and both driving current towards A. Load 4 Ω.
Branch 1 in Norton form: 10/2 = 5 A || 2 Ω
Combine: I_N = 5 + 3 = 8 A,  R_N = 2 || 4 = 1.333 Ω
I_L = 8 × 1.333/(1.333 + 4) = 2 A,  V_L = 2 × 4 = 8 V

Example 3 (dependent source): 12 V source, 4 Ω carrying i_x into node A,
a CCCS draws 0.5·i_x from A to B.
Open circuit: i_x = 0.5 i_x  ->  i_x = 0, so V_oc = 12 V
Short circuit: i_x = 12/4 = 3 A, CCCS takes 1.5 A, I_N = 3 − 1.5 = 1.5 A
R_N = V_oc/I_N = 12/1.5 = 8 Ω   (killing the CCCS would wrongly give 4 Ω)

In AC circuits the Norton current is the phasor short-circuit current and R_N becomes the complex impedance Z_N = Z_th; the conversion I_N = V_th/Z_th needs complex division, so both magnitude and angle change. The load current is then I_N Z_N/(Z_N + Z_L).
Special cases and common mistakes:
items: An ideal current source in series with a resistor is still just that ideal current source; the resistor affects neither I_N nor R_N.
Any resistor connected directly across A-B carries no current when A-B is shorted, but it does appear in R_N.
Dependent sources stay active when finding both I_N and R_N.
The direction of I_N matters: combining two Norton sources that drive opposite ways means subtracting their currents.

concepts.text: The Thevenin and Norton equivalents dissipate different internal power for the same load, so neither can be used to find the efficiency or losses of the original network; they are valid only for what happens at the terminals and in the load.

formulas.latex: I_L = I_N \frac{R_N}{R_N + R_L}, \qquad V_L = I_L R_L
formulas.plainText: I_L = I_N R_N/(R_N + R_L); V_L = I_L R_L

notes.text: Norton and Thevenin share the same resistance; only the source changes. Given one equivalent, the other is one step away: I_N = V_th/R_th or V_th = I_N R_N.

Series versus parallel is the whole point. A current source in series with a resistor, or a voltage source in parallel with one, is never a valid Norton or Thevenin form; such a resistor does not affect the terminals at all.
When finding I_sc, any resistor connected directly across the shorted terminals carries zero current and drops out of the calculation; it reappears when you find R_N.

formulas.title: Norton current
formulas.description: Current through a short circuit placed across the load terminals with all sources active.

formulas.title: Norton resistance
formulas.description: Resistance of the dead network seen from the terminals, identical to the Thevenin resistance.

formulas.title: Thevenin-Norton conversion
formulas.plainText: V_th = I_N R_N; I_N = V_th / R_th
formulas.description: Converts between the two equivalents; the resistance stays the same and moves from series to parallel.

formulas.title: Load current from Norton equivalent
formulas.description: Current-divider rule applied to I_N splitting between R_N and the load R_L.

flashcards.front: How is the Norton current I_N found?
flashcards.back: Short the load terminals and compute the current through the short with all sources active; I_N = I_sc.

flashcards.front: Convert 9 V in series with 3 Ω to its Norton form.
flashcards.back: I_N = 9/3 = 3 A in parallel with the same 3 Ω.

flashcards.front: What is the relation between R_N and R_th?
flashcards.back: They are identical: the resistance of the dead network seen from the terminals, or V_oc/I_sc.

flashcards.front: A Norton source of 5 A in parallel with 6 Ω feeds a 3 Ω load. What is the load current?
flashcards.back: I_L = 5 × 6/(6 + 3) = 3.33 A; the other 1.67 A flows through R_N.

questions.questionText: A network has a Thevenin equivalent of 12 V in series with 3 Ω. Its Norton equivalent is:
questions.explanation: I_N = V_th/R_th = 12/3 = 4 A and R_N = R_th = 3 Ω, connected in parallel with the current source.

questions.questionText: The Norton current of a two-terminal network is obtained by:
options: Open-circuiting the terminals and measuring the terminal current
Dividing the open-circuit voltage by the load resistance
Deactivating all sources and measuring the terminal current
Short-circuiting the terminals and finding the current through the short
questions.explanation: I_N is defined as the short-circuit current I_sc through a zero-resistance link placed across the terminals, with all sources active.

questions.questionText: A Norton equivalent of 6 A in parallel with 8 Ω supplies a 4 Ω load. The load current is:
questions.explanation: Current divider: I_L = I_N × R_N/(R_N + R_L) = 6 × 8/(8 + 4) = 4 A; the remaining 2 A flows through the 8 Ω Norton resistance.

questions.questionText: For the same pair of terminals, the Norton resistance R_N and the Thevenin resistance R_th of a network are related by:
questions.explanation: Both are the resistance of the dead network seen from the terminals, equal to V_oc/I_sc, so they are identical.

questions.questionText: Norton's theorem is the dual of:
questions.explanation: Thevenin uses a voltage source with a series resistance; Norton uses the dual arrangement, a current source with a parallel resistance.

questions.questionText: A Norton equivalent of 5 A in parallel with 4 Ω has its terminals left open. The terminal voltage is:
questions.explanation: With no load, all of I_N flows through R_N: V_oc = I_N R_N = 5 × 4 = 20 V.

questions.questionText: A Norton equivalent of 2.5 A in parallel with 8 Ω is converted to a Thevenin equivalent. The result is:
questions.explanation: V_th = I_N R_N = 2.5 × 8 = 20 V and R_th = R_N = 8 Ω. Dividing (8/2.5 = 3.2 V) or inverting the resistance are slips.

questions.questionText: A 24 V source is in series with 6 Ω to terminal A, and a 3 Ω resistor connects A to terminal B (the source's negative terminal). The Norton equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: Shorting A-B bypasses the 3 Ω, so I_N = 24/6 = 4 A. R_N = 6 || 3 = 2 Ω. 24/9 = 2.67 A wrongly keeps the 3 Ω in the short-circuit path.

questions.questionText: An ideal 10 A current source is in parallel with 5 Ω; a further 5 Ω resistor connects the top of this pair to terminal A, and terminal B is the bottom of the pair. The Norton equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: With A-B shorted the 10 A divides equally between the two 5 Ω paths, so I_N = 10 × 5/(5 + 5) = 5 A. Opening the source gives R_N = 5 + 5 = 10 Ω.

questions.questionText: When the terminals of a Norton equivalent circuit are short-circuited, the current through R_N is:
questions.explanation: The short puts zero volts across R_N, so R_N carries no current and all of I_N flows through the short.

questions.questionText: A Norton equivalent of 10 A in parallel with 10 Ω supplies a 15 Ω load. The power delivered to the load is:
questions.explanation: I_L = 10 × 10/(10 + 15) = 4 A, so P_L = 4² × 15 = 240 W. Using the other branch current (6 A) gives 540 W; 1500 W uses the full I_N.

questions.questionText: A Norton equivalent of 3 A in parallel with 12 Ω supplies a 6 Ω load. The load voltage is:
questions.explanation: R_N and R_L share the same voltage: V_L = I_N × (12 || 6) = 3 × 4 = 12 V. 36 V is the open-circuit voltage.

questions.questionText: Two branches are connected in parallel across terminals A-B: branch 1 is 12 V in series with 4 Ω, branch 2 is 24 V in series with 12 Ω, both with positive terminals towards A. A 7 Ω load is connected across A-B. Using Norton's theorem, the load current is:
questions.explanation: Each branch converts to a Norton source: 12/4 = 3 A and 24/12 = 2 A, so I_N = 5 A with R_N = 4 || 12 = 3 Ω. I_L = 5 × 3/(3 + 7) = 1.5 A.

questions.questionText: A 10 V source in series with 5 Ω delivers current i_x into node A; terminal B is the source's negative terminal. A current-controlled current source between A and B draws 0.5·i_x from A to B. The Norton equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: Short circuit: i_x = 10/5 = 2 A, the dependent source takes 1 A, so I_N = 1 A. Open circuit: i_x = 0.5 i_x forces i_x = 0 and V_oc = 10 V. R_N = 10/1 = 10 Ω; killing the dependent source would wrongly give 5 Ω.

questions.questionText: A 12 V source in series with 3 Ω is connected to terminal A; a 6 Ω resistor and a voltage-controlled current source that draws V_AB/6 amperes from A to B are both connected across A-B (B is the source's negative terminal). The Norton equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: Short circuit: V_AB = 0, so the 6 Ω and the dependent source carry nothing and I_N = 12/3 = 4 A. Open circuit: (12 − V)/3 = V/6 + V/6 gives V_oc = 6 V. R_N = 6/4 = 1.5 Ω; ignoring the dependent source gives 3 || 6 = 2 Ω.

questions.questionText: For which of the following does a Norton equivalent NOT exist?
options: An ideal current source on its own
A current source in parallel with a resistor
An ideal voltage source on its own
questions.explanation: An ideal voltage source has zero internal resistance, so its short-circuit current is infinite and it cannot be written as a finite I_N in parallel with R_N.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the Thevenin and Norton equivalents of the same network is NOT correct?
options: The power dissipated inside the two equivalents is always equal for the same load
Both deliver the same current to any load
I_N × R_N equals the open-circuit voltage
questions.explanation: The two are equivalent only at the terminals. With the terminals open, for instance, R_th dissipates nothing while R_N dissipates I_N²R_N.

questions.questionText: A Norton equivalent of 2 A in parallel with 10 Ω has its terminals open. The power dissipated inside R_N is:
questions.explanation: With no load all 2 A flows in R_N: P = 2² × 10 = 40 W. The Thevenin equivalent would dissipate 0 W in the same condition.

questions.questionText: As the Norton resistance R_N of a source becomes very large compared with the load, the source behaves more and more like:
options: An open circuit with no output
questions.explanation: When R_N ≫ R_L almost all of I_N flows into the load whatever its value, which is the behaviour of an ideal current source.

questions.questionText: A current source of 10 mA with a Norton resistance of 100 kΩ supplies a 1 kΩ load. The load current is:
questions.explanation: I_L = 10 × 100/(100 + 1) = 9.90 mA. Because R_N ≫ R_L nearly the whole source current reaches the load; 0.099 mA uses the wrong resistor in the divider.

questions.questionText: A Norton equivalent of 8 A in parallel with 6 Ω is to deliver 2 A to a load. The load resistance required is:
questions.explanation: 2 = 8 × 6/(6 + R_L) gives 6 + R_L = 24, so R_L = 18 Ω. Taking 24 Ω forgets to subtract R_N.

questions.questionText: A 12 V source feeds two parallel arms. Arm 1 is 2 Ω (top) in series with 4 Ω (bottom); arm 2 is 4 Ω (top) in series with 2 Ω (bottom). The Norton equivalent seen between the two arm midpoints is:
questions.explanation: V_oc = 12 × 4/6 − 12 × 2/6 = 8 − 4 = 4 V. With the source shorted, R_N = (2 || 4) + (4 || 2) = 1.333 + 1.333 = 2.67 Ω, so I_N = 4/2.67 = 1.5 A. 4.5 A is the total source current with the midpoints shorted.

questions.questionText: The Norton form of a network is especially convenient when:
options: The load is connected in series with an ideal voltage source
Several loads or branches are connected in parallel across the terminals
The network contains no resistors at all
Only the internal losses of the original network are needed
questions.explanation: In parallel the voltage is common and branch currents add, so a current source with a parallel resistance combines directly with parallel loads and with nodal analysis.

questions.questionText: Two Norton sources are connected in parallel with the same polarity: 4 A in parallel with 6 Ω, and 2 A in parallel with 3 Ω. The combined Norton equivalent is:
questions.explanation: Parallel current sources add: I_N = 4 + 2 = 6 A. The resistances are in parallel: 6 || 3 = 2 Ω. 9 Ω is the series mistake and 2 A would apply only if the sources opposed.

questions.questionText: A 5 A source in parallel with 10 Ω and a 3 A source in parallel with 10 Ω are connected across the same terminals with the two current sources driving in opposite directions. A 5 Ω load is connected across the terminals. The load current is:
questions.explanation: Opposing sources subtract: I_N = 5 − 3 = 2 A, with R_N = 10 || 10 = 5 Ω. I_L = 2 × 5/(5 + 5) = 1 A. Adding the currents (8 A) gives 4 A.

questions.questionText: When the terminals of a Norton equivalent are left open, the terminal voltage equals:
questions.explanation: With no external path, all of I_N flows through R_N, so the open-circuit voltage is I_N R_N, which is also V_th.

questions.questionText: While calculating the Norton current, a resistor that is connected directly across the terminals A-B:
options: Carries no current and drops out of the I_N calculation
Must be moved in series with the source
questions.explanation: The short across A-B also shorts that resistor, so it carries zero current. It does, however, appear in parallel when R_N is found.

questions.questionText: An ideal 2 A current source in series with a 50 Ω resistor is connected to terminals A-B. As seen from A-B, this combination is equivalent to:
options: An ideal 2 A current source alone
questions.explanation: An ideal current source forces 2 A whatever is in series with it, so the 50 Ω has no effect on the terminals and R_N is infinite. A source transformation applies only to a parallel resistor.

questions.questionText: An ideal ammeter connected across terminals A-B of a linear network reads 3 A, and an ideal voltmeter across the same terminals reads 18 V. The Norton equivalent is:
questions.explanation: The ammeter reads I_sc = I_N = 3 A and the voltmeter reads V_oc = 18 V, so R_N = 18/3 = 6 Ω.

questions.questionText: A 30 V source is in series with 5 Ω to node X. A 20 Ω resistor connects X to terminal B (the source's negative terminal), and a 4 Ω resistor runs from X to terminal A. The Norton equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: Short A-B: 4 || 20 = 3.33 Ω, total 8.33 Ω, source current 30/8.33 = 3.6 A, of which 3.6 × 20/24 = 3 A flows in the short. R_N = (5 || 20) + 4 = 8 Ω. Check: V_oc = 30 × 20/25 = 24 V = 3 × 8.

questions.questionText: An ideal 4 A current source injects current into node A from terminal B. Also connected are a 6 Ω resistor from A to B and a 12 V source in series with 3 Ω from B to A (positive towards A). A 6 Ω load is connected across A-B. Using Norton's theorem, the load current is:
questions.explanation: Short A-B: the 6 Ω is bypassed, I_N = 4 + 12/3 = 8 A. R_N = 6 || 3 = 2 Ω. I_L = 8 × 2/(2 + 6) = 2 A; 2.67 A (8 × 2/6) wrongly divides by R_L alone instead of R_N + R_L.

questions.questionText: When a Thevenin equivalent is converted to its Norton form, the arrow of the Norton current source:
options: Points towards the terminal that is negative in the Thevenin form
Can be drawn in either direction
Points towards the terminal that is positive in the Thevenin form
questions.explanation: I_N is the current that would flow out of the positive terminal into a short circuit, so the source must push current towards that terminal.

questions.questionText: In a Norton equivalent with a load connected across its terminals, R_N and the load always have the same:
questions.explanation: R_N and R_L are in parallel, so they share one voltage while I_N divides between them.

questions.questionText: A network has a Thevenin equivalent of 50∠0° V in series with (3 + j4) Ω. Its Norton equivalent is:
options: 10∠53.13° A in parallel with (3 + j4) Ω
10∠−53.13° A in parallel with (3 + j4) Ω
7.14∠0° A in parallel with (3 + j4) Ω
questions.explanation: I_N = V_th/Z_th = 50∠0°/(5∠53.13°) = 10∠−53.13° A, and Z_N = Z_th = 3 + j4 Ω. 7.14 A comes from wrongly adding 3 + 4 = 7 Ω.

questions.questionText: A 100∠0° V source is in series with a 10 Ω resistor, and a capacitive reactance of −j10 Ω is connected across terminals A-B at the far end. The Norton equivalent at A-B is:
options: 10∠0° A in parallel with (10 − j10) Ω
7.07∠45° A in parallel with (5 − j5) Ω
10∠0° A in parallel with (5 + j5) Ω
10∠0° A in parallel with (5 − j5) Ω
questions.explanation: Shorting A-B bypasses the capacitor: I_N = 100/10 = 10∠0° A. Z_N = 10 || (−j10) = −j100/(10 − j10) = 5 − j5 Ω. 7.07∠45° A is the source current with the capacitor left in circuit.

questions.questionText: When finding the Norton current of a circuit that contains a dependent source, the dependent source is:
questions.explanation: Dependent sources are never killed; their values change with the circuit conditions and must be recalculated with the terminals shorted.

questions.questionText: A Norton equivalent of 12 mA in parallel with 2 kΩ supplies a 2 kΩ load. The load voltage is:
questions.explanation: The parallel combination is 2 || 2 = 1 kΩ, so V_L = 12 mA × 1 kΩ = 12 V. 24 V is the open-circuit voltage.

questions.questionText: A linear network delivers 2 A into a short circuit across its terminals and 1.5 A into a 4 Ω load. Its Norton resistance is:
questions.explanation: I_N = 2 A. Then 1.5 = 2 × R_N/(R_N + 4) gives 1.5R_N + 6 = 2R_N, so R_N = 12 Ω. Check: V_oc = 24 V, 24/(12 + 4) = 1.5 A.

questions.questionText: A Norton equivalent of 9 A in parallel with 3 Ω supplies a 6 Ω load. The current flowing through R_N is:
questions.explanation: By the current divider, I_RN = 9 × 6/(3 + 6) = 6 A; the load takes the other 3 A. The smaller resistance takes the larger share.

questions.questionText: If the load resistance is much smaller than the Norton resistance (R_L ≪ R_N), the load current is approximately:
questions.explanation: I_L = I_N R_N/(R_N + R_L) → I_N when R_L ≪ R_N: nearly all the current takes the low-resistance path.

questions.questionText: A 12 V battery has an internal resistance of 0.05 Ω. Its Norton equivalent is:
questions.explanation: I_N = V/R = 12/0.05 = 240 A in parallel with the same 0.05 Ω; this is also the battery's short-circuit current. 0.6 A multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.questionText: A 20 V source in series with 10 Ω is connected to terminal A; terminal B is its negative terminal. Also across A-B are a 10 Ω resistor and an ideal 1 A current source that draws current out of A into B. The Norton equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: Short A-B: the source branch gives 20/10 = 2 A and the current source removes 1 A, so I_N = 1 A. R_N = 10 || 10 = 5 Ω (current source opened).

questions.questionText: The open-circuit voltage of a linear network is 30 V. A 10 Ω load connected to it draws 2 A. The Norton equivalent of the network is:
questions.explanation: 2 = 30/(R + 10) gives R = 5 Ω, so I_N = V_oc/R = 30/5 = 6 A in parallel with 5 Ω. Using the load current as I_N or 30/10 = 3 A are common mistakes.

questions.questionText: Which statement about Norton's theorem is NOT correct?
options: The Norton current depends on the value of the load resistance
R_N is equal to the Thevenin resistance
It applies to linear bilateral networks
questions.explanation: I_N is the short-circuit current with the load removed, a property of the network alone; only the load's share of it depends on R_L.

questions.questionText: An ideal 6 A current source, a 3 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are all connected in parallel across terminals A-B. The Norton equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: The circuit is already in Norton form: I_N = 6 A (both resistors are bypassed by the short) and R_N = 3 || 6 = 2 Ω.

questions.questionText: A 20 V source is in series with 4 Ω to node X; a 4 Ω resistor connects X to terminal B (the source's negative terminal), an ideal 3 A current source injects current into X from B, and a 2 Ω resistor runs from X to terminal A. The Norton equivalent at A-B is:
questions.explanation: Short A-B, nodal at X: (20 − V)/4 + 3 = V/4 + V/2 gives 8 = V, so I_N = 8/2 = 4 A. R_N = (4 || 4) + 2 = 4 Ω. Check: V_oc from (20 − V)/4 + 3 = V/4 is 16 V = 4 × 4. Ignoring the 3 A source gives 2.5 A.

questions.questionText: For a fixed Norton equivalent, as the load resistance is increased, the current through R_N:
options: Stays equal to the load current
questions.explanation: I_RN = I_N R_L/(R_N + R_L), which grows with R_L; on open circuit all of I_N flows in R_N.

questions.questionText: In small-signal analysis the output of a BJT amplifier is often modelled as a controlled current source g_m·v_be in parallel with an output resistance r_o. This model is an example of:
options: A superposition of two independent sources
questions.explanation: A current source with a parallel resistance is the Norton form; it suits the transistor because the collector current is nearly independent of the load.

questions.questionText: A network with V_th = 15 V and R_th = 2.5 Ω is converted to Norton form and then connected to a 5 Ω load. The load current is:
questions.explanation: I_N = 15/2.5 = 6 A in parallel with 2.5 Ω. I_L = 6 × 2.5/(2.5 + 5) = 2 A, the same as 15/(2.5 + 5) from the Thevenin form. 4 A uses the wrong resistor in the divider.

subtopics.title: Maximum Power Transfer Theorem
subtopics.subtitle: Load receives the most power when R_L = R_th, but efficiency is then only 50 %

concepts.text: Statement

A source, or any linear network reduced to its Thevenin equivalent V_th and R_th, delivers maximum power to a resistive load when the load resistance equals the Thevenin (source) resistance: R_L = R_th. The theorem applies to a fixed source and an adjustable load. If instead the load is fixed and the source resistance can be chosen, load power is maximised by making the source resistance as small as possible.
Derivation Outline
Starting from the Thevenin equivalent with load R_L:
items: Load current I = V_th/(R_th + R_L), so load power P_L = I²R_L = V_th² R_L/(R_th + R_L)².
Set dP_L/dR_L = 0: (R_th + R_L)² − 2R_L(R_th + R_L) = 0, which gives R_L = R_th.
Substituting R_L = R_th gives P_max = V_th²/(4R_th). In Norton form, with V_th = I_N R_N, P_max = I_N² R_N/4.

concepts.plainText: Pmax = Vth² / (4 Rth)
Pmax = I_N² R_N / 4

concepts.text: Efficiency at Maximum Power

At R_L = R_th the same current flows through R_th and R_L, so as much power is lost inside the source as is delivered to the load: efficiency η = R_L/(R_th + R_L) = 50 %. Power systems therefore never operate at matched load; they keep R_th much smaller than R_L so that efficiency approaches 100 %. Communication, audio and antenna circuits accept the 50 % efficiency because extracting the largest possible signal power matters more than wasting a little source power.

concepts.plainText: η = R_L / (R_th + R_L) = 1/2 (50 %) when R_L = R_th

concepts.text: AC Circuits

For an AC source with Thevenin impedance Z_th = R_th + jX_th, maximum power is delivered to a load equal to the complex conjugate, Z_L = Z_th* = R_th − jX_th: the reactances cancel and the resistances match. If the load must be purely resistive, the best choice is R_L = |Z_th| = √(R_th² + X_th²). If only the magnitude of a fixed-angle load can be varied, choose |Z_L| = |Z_th|.

concepts.plainText: Z_L = conjugate of Z_th = R_th − jX_th

concepts.text: Applications
Impedance matching, where signal power counts more than efficiency:
items: Audio systems: matching an amplifier output to a loudspeaker, often through an output transformer.
Communication circuits: matching a transmitter or receiver to its antenna and transmission line.
Matching transformers, which make a load look like R_th to the source (turns ratio √(R_th/R_L)).
Solar photovoltaic systems: maximum-power-point tracking keeps the panel at its optimum load.

concepts.text: Worked Example

A source of 20 V with internal resistance 5 Ω feeds a variable load. For maximum power choose R_L = 5 Ω: I = 20/(5 + 5) = 2 A and P_max = 20²/(4 × 5) = 20 W; the source resistance also dissipates 2² × 5 = 20 W, so the efficiency is 50 %. With R_L = 15 Ω instead, I = 1 A, P_L = 15 W and efficiency = 15/20 = 75 %: less power to the load, but a higher fraction of the total.
Going Deeper: Maximum Power Transfer

The load power has a peak because two effects pull in opposite directions. A small load resistance draws a large current but develops almost no voltage, while a large load resistance develops nearly the full V_th but draws almost no current. Writing x = R_L/R_th turns the load-power equation into a single universal curve, P_L/P_max = 4x/(1 + x)², which is the same for every source. The curve is flat near its peak, so a moderate mismatch costs surprisingly little power.

concepts.plainText: P_L / Pmax = 4x / (1 + x)², where x = R_L / R_th

concepts.text: The table shows a useful pairing rule: two loads R1 and R2 with R1 × R2 = R_th² receive exactly the same power, one below and one above the peak (0.5 and 2, or 0.25 and 4, in the table). To find the loads that receive a chosen fraction k of P_max, set 4x/(1 + x)² = k and solve the quadratic k x² + (2k − 4) x + k = 0; its two roots are always reciprocals of each other. Efficiency, on the other hand, keeps rising with R_L, so a designer who wants both reasonable power and good efficiency chooses R_L a few times larger than R_th.

Example 1: 48 V source, 8 Ω in series, 24 Ω across the output,
then 4 Ω in series to terminals a-b. Find R_L and P_max.
V_th = 48 × 24/(8 + 24) = 36 V   (open-circuit voltage of the divider)
R_th = (8 ∥ 24) + 4 = 6 + 4 = 10 Ω   (source replaced by a short)
Choose R_L = R_th = 10 Ω
I = V_th/(2R_th) = 36/20 = 1.8 A
P_max = V_th²/(4R_th) = 1296/40 = 32.4 W
Check: I²R_L = 1.8² × 10 = 32.4 W

Example 2: 120 V rms, 50 Hz source with Z_th = 8 + j6 Ω.
(a) Conjugate load: Z_L = 8 − j6 Ω, i.e. 8 Ω with a capacitor of X_C = 6 Ω
    C = 1/(2π × 50 × 6) = 530.5 µF
    Total Z = 16 Ω (reactances cancel), I = 120/16 = 7.5 A
    P = V²/(4R_th) = 14400/32 = 450 W
(b) Purely resistive load: R_L = |Z_th| = √(8² + 6²) = 10 Ω
    |Z_total| = |18 + j6| = 18.97 Ω, I = 120/18.97 = 6.325 A
    P = I²R_L = 40 × 10 = 400 W   (less than the 450 W of case a)
Common mistakes in maximum power problems:
items: Using V_th²/R_th or V_th²/(2R_th) instead of V_th²/(4R_th); these give four and two times the true answer.
Matching the load to the source EMF's own internal resistance while ignoring other resistors in the network; always find R_th at the load terminals.
Setting dependent sources to zero when finding R_th; only independent sources are removed.
Taking Z_L = Z_th instead of its conjugate in AC problems; the reactances must cancel, not add.
Applying R_L = R_th when the load is fixed and the source resistance is the variable; then R_s should be as small as possible.
Mixing peak and rms values: with a peak amplitude V_m the matched power is V_m²/(8R_th).

concepts.text: Special cases are handled with the same idea. When a network contains dependent sources, R_th is found from the ratio V_oc/I_sc or by applying a test source with the independent sources removed, and the maximum power follows directly from the two terminal measurements. When a fixed resistor sits in series with the variable load, it is simply absorbed into the source side, so the variable part must equal R_th plus that fixed resistance. For a sinusoidal source, the conjugate-matched power is V_th²/(4R_th) with rms values, and the reactance of the source never dissipates power.

concepts.plainText: Pmax = V_oc × I_sc / 4, with R_th = V_oc / I_sc

concepts.text: Before computing, ask two questions: which element is variable (load or source), and is the load allowed to have reactance? A variable resistive load on a DC network gives R_L = R_th; a fully adjustable AC load gives Z_th*; a resistive AC load gives |Z_th|; a variable source resistance gives R_s = 0.

formulas.plainText: AC: Z_L = complex conjugate of Z_th

notes.text: Whenever V_th and R_th are given and the maximum load power is asked, the answer is V_th²/4R_th. Remember the 4 (not 2): half the voltage appears across the load, and half the total power reaches it.
Maximum power transfer and maximum efficiency are different goals. At matched load efficiency is only 50 %; as R_L → ∞ efficiency → 100 % but the load power → 0.
Conjugate matching in AC means equal resistance and equal-but-opposite reactance. A common exam variant: 'source 4 + j3 Ω, purely resistive load' has the answer R_L = |Z_th| = 5 Ω, not 4 Ω.

formulas.title: Maximum power condition
formulas.description: Load resistance must equal the Thevenin (source) resistance for the load to receive maximum power.

formulas.title: Maximum power
formulas.description: Power delivered to a matched load; V_th, R_th from the Thevenin equivalent or I_N, R_N from the Norton equivalent.

formulas.title: Load power for any R_L
formulas.description: General load power; differentiate with respect to R_L to prove the theorem.

formulas.title: Efficiency of power transfer
formulas.description: Fraction of the total generated power that reaches the load; equals 0.5 (50 %) at R_L = R_th.

formulas.title: AC conjugate matching
formulas.description: Load impedance for maximum power from an AC source with Thevenin impedance R_th + jX_th; use |Z_th| if the load must be resistive.

flashcards.front: A source has V_th = 10 V and R_th = 2 Ω. What is the maximum power it can deliver to a load?
flashcards.back: P_max = 10²/(4 × 2) = 12.5 W, obtained with R_L = 2 Ω.

flashcards.front: Why is the efficiency only 50 % at maximum power transfer?
flashcards.back: With R_L = R_th the same current flows through both, so the source resistance dissipates exactly as much power as the load receives.

flashcards.front: Which load impedance draws maximum power from an AC source with Z_th = 4 + j3 Ω?
flashcards.back: The complex conjugate Z_L = 4 − j3 Ω. If the load must be resistive, R_L = |Z_th| = 5 Ω.

questions.questionText: A DC source has an open-circuit voltage of 24 V and an internal resistance of 6 Ω. What is the maximum power it can deliver to a variable resistive load?
questions.explanation: P_max = V_th²/(4R_th) = 24²/(4 × 6) = 576/24 = 24 W, obtained with R_L = 6 Ω. 96 W is V²/R and 48 W is V²/2R.

questions.questionText: A 30 V source with 5 Ω internal resistance is connected to a load adjusted for maximum power transfer. What current flows in the load?
questions.explanation: For maximum power R_L = 5 Ω, so I = V/(R_s + R_L) = 30/(5 + 5) = 3 A. Dividing 30 V by 5 Ω alone (6 A) forgets the load resistance.

questions.questionText: Under maximum power transfer conditions in a DC circuit, the voltage across the load is:
options: One quarter of the Thevenin voltage
questions.explanation: With R_L = R_th the Thevenin voltage divides equally between R_th and R_L, so V_L = V_th/2.

questions.questionText: The maximum power transfer condition R_L = R_th answers which design question?
options: Which source resistance delivers the most power to a given, fixed load
How to make the efficiency of power transfer 100 %
Which load resistance extracts the most power from a given, fixed source network
How to find the current in every branch of a network
questions.explanation: The theorem assumes the source network, and hence V_th and R_th, is fixed while the load is varied. For a fixed load with adjustable source resistance, the best source resistance is as small as possible.

questions.questionText: A Norton equivalent consists of a 4 A current source in parallel with 10 Ω. What maximum power can it deliver to a load?
questions.explanation: P_max = I_N²R_N/4 = 4² × 10/4 = 40 W, with R_L = 10 Ω. 160 W is I_N²R_N, which forgets that only half of I_N flows in the matched load.

questions.questionText: When a load is matched for maximum power transfer, the power dissipated in the source's internal resistance is:
options: Equal to the power delivered to the load
questions.explanation: The same current flows through R_th and R_L, and the two resistances are equal, so I²R_th = I²R_L: the internal loss equals the load power.

questions.questionText: As the load resistance connected to a fixed source is increased from zero to a very large value, the power delivered to the load:
options: Rises from zero to a peak at R_L = R_th and then falls towards zero
questions.explanation: At R_L = 0 the load voltage is zero and as R_L → ∞ the current is zero, so the load power is zero at both ends with a single peak at R_L = R_th.

questions.questionText: An AC source has Thevenin impedance Z_th = R_th + jX_th. If both the resistance and the reactance of the load can be adjusted freely, maximum power is delivered when Z_L equals:
questions.explanation: The complex conjugate Z_th* = R_th − jX_th cancels the source reactance and matches the resistance, giving P_max = V_th²/(4R_th).

questions.questionText: In which of these situations is operating at maximum power transfer (a matched load) desirable?
options: Connecting a radio receiver's input stage to its antenna
Transmitting bulk power from a generating station to a city
Supplying household lighting from the mains
Feeding an industrial motor from a distribution transformer
questions.explanation: Weak signals in communication circuits need the largest possible power, so the 50 % efficiency is acceptable. Power supply systems need high efficiency and are deliberately not matched.

questions.questionText: A 12 V battery has an internal resistance of 0.5 Ω. Which load resistance draws maximum power, and what is that power?
questions.explanation: R_L = r = 0.5 Ω and P_max = 12²/(4 × 0.5) = 144/2 = 72 W. 288 W is V²/r and 144 W is V²/(2r).

questions.questionText: As the load resistance R_L connected to a fixed source is made very much larger than R_th, the efficiency of power transfer:
options: Approaches 100 % and the load power becomes maximum
Approaches 100 % while the load power approaches zero
questions.explanation: η = R_L/(R_th + R_L) tends to 1 as R_L → ∞, but the current, and therefore the load power, tends to zero.

questions.questionText: A source with internal resistance R_th feeds a load R_L = 3R_th. What is the efficiency of power transfer?
To apply the maximum power transfer theorem to a complicated network, the part of the network seen by the load is first replaced by its:
options: Superposition equivalent with all sources removed
Series sum of all the resistors in the network
questions.explanation: The theorem is stated for a source V_th in series with R_th (or I_N with R_N), so the network at the load terminals is reduced to its Thevenin or Norton equivalent first.

questions.questionText: In the expression P_max = V_th²/(4R_th), the quantity V_th is:
options: The voltage across the load when it is matched
The source EMF multiplied by the load current
The open-circuit voltage at the load terminals with the load removed
The voltage across R_th at maximum power
questions.explanation: V_th is the open-circuit voltage at the load terminals. At matching, the load voltage (and the drop across R_th) is only V_th/2.

questions.questionText: A 1.5 V cell has an internal resistance of 0.3 Ω. What is the maximum power it can deliver to an external resistor?
questions.explanation: P_max = E²/(4r) = 1.5²/(4 × 0.3) = 2.25/1.2 = 1.875 W, with a 0.3 Ω load. 7.5 W is E²/r and 3.75 W is E²/(2r).

questions.questionText: A source with V_th = 50 V and R_th = 10 Ω supplies a 40 Ω load. What power does the load receive?
questions.explanation: I = 50/(10 + 40) = 1 A, so P_L = I²R_L = 1² × 40 = 40 W. This is below P_max = 50²/(4 × 10) = 62.5 W because the load is not matched; 50 W is the total power and 10 W the internal loss.

questions.questionText: A source delivers a maximum of 18 W to a matched load. If its internal resistance is 8 Ω, what is its open-circuit voltage?
questions.explanation: From P_max = V_th²/(4R_th): V_th = √(4 × 8 × 18) = √576 = 24 V. 12 V is √(P R) and 17 V is √(2PR).

questions.questionText: An AC source of 100 V (rms) has an internal impedance of 3 + j4 Ω. What is the maximum power it can deliver to a conjugate-matched load?
questions.explanation: With Z_L = 3 − j4 Ω the reactances cancel, so P_max = V²/(4R_th) = 100²/(4 × 3) = 10000/12 = 833.3 W. Using |Z_th| = 5 Ω instead of R_th gives the wrong 500 W.

questions.questionText: An AC source has Z_th = 6 + j8 Ω. If the load must be a pure resistor, what value receives maximum power?
questions.explanation: For a purely resistive load, R_L = |Z_th| = √(6² + 8²) = 10 Ω. 6 Ω would be correct only if the load could also cancel the reactance.

questions.questionText: A source has R_th = 10 Ω. Load resistors of 4 Ω and 25 Ω are connected to it one at a time. How do the two load powers compare?
options: The 4 Ω load receives more power
The 25 Ω load receives more power
They cannot be compared without knowing V_th
questions.explanation: P_L ∝ R_L/(R_th + R_L)²: 4/14² = 0.0204 and 25/35² = 0.0204. Whenever R1 × R2 = R_th² (here 4 × 25 = 100 = 10²) the two loads receive equal power, one on each side of the peak.

questions.questionText: For a linear network that contains dependent sources, the load resistance for maximum power transfer is best found as:
options: The sum of all the resistances in the network
R_L = V_oc/I_sc, the ratio of open-circuit voltage to short-circuit current at the load terminals
The resistance seen with all sources, dependent and independent, set to zero
The resistance of the element nearest to the load terminals
questions.explanation: Dependent sources must stay active when finding R_th, so it is obtained from V_oc/I_sc or with a test source; the matched load is then R_L = R_th.

questions.questionText: Measurements at a pair of terminals give an open-circuit voltage of 20 V and a short-circuit current of 4 A. What maximum power can the network deliver to a load?
questions.explanation: R_th = V_oc/I_sc = 20/4 = 5 Ω, so P_max = V_oc²/(4R_th) = 400/20 = 20 W, which equals V_oc × I_sc/4.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a load matched for maximum power transfer is NOT correct?
options: The load voltage is half the open-circuit voltage
The load current is half the short-circuit current
The efficiency of power transfer is at its highest possible value
The power lost in R_th equals the load power
questions.explanation: At matching the efficiency is only 50 %; it keeps rising as R_L increases. The other three statements all follow from R_L = R_th.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with an output resistance of 800 Ω must deliver maximum power to an 8 Ω loudspeaker through an ideal transformer. The required turns ratio N1 : N2 (amplifier side : speaker side) is:
questions.explanation: The load is reflected as (N1/N2)² R_L, so (N1/N2)² = 800/8 = 100 and N1/N2 = 10. The answer 100 : 1 forgets the square root.

questions.questionText: An 8 Ω loudspeaker is connected to the secondary of an ideal transformer with turns ratio N1 : N2 = 4 : 1. What resistance does the amplifier see at the primary?
questions.explanation: Reflected resistance = (N1/N2)² × R_L = 4² × 8 = 128 Ω. Multiplying by the ratio instead of its square gives 32 Ω.

questions.questionText: A load resistance R_L is fixed, and the internal resistance R_s of the source can be chosen. For maximum power in the load, R_s should be:
questions.explanation: P_L = V²R_L/(R_s + R_L)² always increases as R_s decreases, so the best source resistance is zero. R_s = R_L applies only when the load is the variable.

questions.questionText: A fixed 10 Ω load is fed from a 20 V source whose internal resistance can be set anywhere between 0 and 10 Ω. What is the greatest load power obtainable?
questions.explanation: With the load fixed, choose R_s = 0: P = V²/R_L = 20²/10 = 40 W. Setting R_s = R_L = 10 Ω would give only 20²/40 = 10 W.

questions.questionText: A load resistance equal to twice the Thevenin resistance (R_L = 2R_th) receives what percentage of the maximum available power?
questions.explanation: P_L/P_max = 4x/(1 + x)² with x = 2: 8/9 = 0.889 = 88.9 %. 66.7 % is the efficiency at this load, not the power ratio.

questions.questionText: Why are electric power transmission and distribution systems NOT operated under maximum power transfer conditions?
options: Generators cannot deliver current into a matched load
Matching makes the power factor zero
Half of the generated power would be lost in the source and network
A matched load draws no current from the supply
questions.explanation: At matched load the efficiency is only 50 %, which is unacceptable for bulk power. Power systems keep source and line impedances much smaller than the load so efficiency is high.

questions.questionText: An AC source with Thevenin impedance Z_th feeds a load whose phase angle is fixed but whose magnitude |Z_L| can be varied. Maximum power is transferred when:
questions.explanation: When only the magnitude of a fixed-angle load can change, maximum load power occurs at |Z_L| = |Z_th|; the purely resistive load R_L = |Z_th| is a special case.

questions.questionText: A 60 V source with 10 Ω internal resistance feeds a fixed 5 Ω resistor in series with a variable resistor R. For maximum power in R, the value of R and that power are:
questions.explanation: The fixed 5 Ω joins the source side, so R_th = 10 + 5 = 15 Ω. Then R = 15 Ω and P = 60²/(4 × 15) = 60 W; using R_th = 10 Ω gives the wrong 90 W.

questions.questionText: In a solar photovoltaic system, a maximum power point tracker (MPPT) continuously:
options: Adjusts the effective load seen by the panel so that the product V × I delivered by the panel is maximised
Holds the panel output current at its short-circuit value
Holds the panel output voltage at its open-circuit value
Disconnects the load whenever the efficiency falls below 50 %
questions.explanation: Panel power is zero at both short circuit (V = 0) and open circuit (I = 0). The MPPT converter varies the load it presents so the panel stays at the knee where V × I is largest.

questions.questionText: A source with V_th = 40 V and R_th = 8 Ω is matched to its load. What is the total power generated by the source (load power plus internal loss)?
questions.explanation: I = 40/(8 + 8) = 2.5 A, so total power = V_th × I = 40 × 2.5 = 100 W; the load gets 50 W and R_th dissipates 50 W.

questions.questionText: A source of fixed EMF 20 V has its internal resistance increased from 5 Ω to 10 Ω. The maximum power it can deliver to a matched load changes from:
questions.explanation: P_max = V²/(4R_th): 400/20 = 20 W before and 400/40 = 10 W after. P_max is inversely proportional to R_th, so doubling R_th halves it.

questions.questionText: A Norton source has I_N = 0.5 A and delivers a maximum of 5 W to a matched load. What is its Norton resistance R_N?
questions.explanation: From P_max = I_N²R_N/4: R_N = 4P_max/I_N² = 4 × 5/0.25 = 80 Ω. Omitting the factor 4 gives 20 Ω.

questions.questionText: An AC source of 20 V (rms) with internal impedance 2 + j5 Ω is conjugate matched to its load. What is the rms load current?
questions.explanation: Total impedance = (2 + j5) + (2 − j5) = 4 Ω, so I = 20/4 = 5 A and the load power is 5² × 2 = 50 W. 3.71 A would be 20/|Z_th|.

questions.questionText: Which statement about maximum power transfer in a linear DC network is correct?
options: The maximum load power depends only on V_th and R_th, not on the internal arrangement of the network
The load receives all of the power produced by the sources
For a Norton source the condition becomes R_L = 2R_N
At maximum power the load current equals the short-circuit current
questions.explanation: Any linear network looks like V_th in series with R_th at its terminals, so P_max = V_th²/(4R_th) whatever is inside. For a Norton source the condition is R_L = R_N and the load current is I_sc/2.

questions.questionText: A 36 V source in series with 6 Ω feeds a 12 Ω resistor connected across the output terminals. A variable load R_L is connected across the 12 Ω resistor. What maximum power can R_L receive?
questions.explanation: V_th = 36 × 12/(6 + 12) = 24 V and R_th = 6 ∥ 12 = 4 Ω, so P_max = 24²/(4 × 4) = 36 W. Ignoring the 12 Ω shunt gives 36²/24 = 54 W.

questions.questionText: An AC source of 100 V (rms) has internal impedance 6 + j8 Ω and feeds a purely resistive load chosen for maximum power. What power does the load receive?
questions.explanation: R_L = |Z_th| = 10 Ω; |Z_total| = |16 + j8| = 17.89 Ω, I = 100/17.89 = 5.59 A, P = 5.59² × 10 = 312.5 W. 416.7 W would need a conjugate load.

questions.questionText: A 100 V source with internal resistance 20 Ω must supply its load at 80 % efficiency. What load resistance is needed, and what power does the load receive?
questions.explanation: η = R_L/(R_th + R_L) = 0.8 gives R_L = 4R_th = 80 Ω. Then I = 100/(20 + 80) = 1 A and P_L = 1² × 80 = 80 W, less than P_max = 125 W.

questions.questionText: A source delivers 2 A into a 10 Ω load and 1.5 A into a 15 Ω load. What is the maximum power it can deliver to any resistive load?
questions.explanation: E = 2(r + 10) = 1.5(r + 15) gives r = 5 Ω and E = 30 V, so P_max = 30²/(4 × 5) = 45 W. 40 W and 33.75 W are just the powers in the two test loads.

questions.questionText: A 3 A current source in parallel with 12 Ω is followed by a 4 Ω series resistor leading to the load terminals. What maximum power can a load draw?
questions.explanation: Source transformation: 3 A ∥ 12 Ω = 36 V in series with 12 Ω, so V_th = 36 V and R_th = 12 + 4 = 16 Ω. P_max = 36²/(4 × 16) = 1296/64 = 20.25 W.

questions.questionText: A 20 V source feeds two parallel voltage dividers: branch A is 4 Ω (top) and 6 Ω (bottom); branch B is 6 Ω (top) and 4 Ω (bottom). A variable load is connected between the two midpoints. What maximum power can the load receive?
A 50 V (rms), 50 Hz source has internal impedance 10 + j20 Ω. The load for maximum power is a resistor in series with a capacitor. Their values are:
questions.explanation: The conjugate load is 10 − j20 Ω: R = 10 Ω and X_C = 20 Ω, so C = 1/(2π × 50 × 20) = 159 µF. 63.7 mH is an inductor of 20 Ω, which would add to the source reactance instead of cancelling it.

questions.questionText: Two batteries are connected in parallel to feed a common load: one of 10 V with 2 Ω internal resistance and one of 16 V with 4 Ω internal resistance. What maximum power can the combination deliver to a load resistor?
A load is set to R_L = R_th/4. What fraction of the maximum available power does it receive, and what is the efficiency of transfer?
A source has R_th = 6 Ω. Which pair of load resistances each receives exactly 75 % of the maximum available power?
questions.explanation: Set 4x/(1 + x)² = 0.75: 3x² − 10x + 3 = 0, so x = 1/3 or 3, i.e. R_L = 2 Ω or 18 Ω (note 2 × 18 = 6²). The pair 3 Ω and 12 Ω each receive 88.9 %.

subtopics.title: R-L, R-C, R-L-C Circuits
subtopics.subtitle: Reactance, impedance, phase angle and time constants of single-phase AC circuits

concepts.text: Reactance

In AC circuits, inductors and capacitors oppose current with frequency-dependent reactance instead of fixed resistance. Reactance is measured in ohms, but unlike resistance it stores energy during one part of the cycle and returns it during the next, so it dissipates no average power.

concepts.latex: X_L = 2\pi f L, \qquad X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}
concepts.plainText: XL = 2 pi f L; XC = 1/(2 pi f C)

concepts.text: Behaviour with frequency:
items: X_L rises with frequency: an inductor blocks high frequencies and passes DC (X_L = 0 at f = 0).
X_C falls with frequency: a capacitor blocks DC and low frequencies (X_C = ∞ at f = 0).
In a pure inductor, current LAGS voltage by 90°.
In a pure capacitor, current LEADS voltage by 90° (mnemonic CIVIL: in C, I leads V; V leads I in L).

concepts.text: Series R-L Circuit

The same current I flows through R and L. V_R = IR is in phase with I, while V_L = IX_L leads I by 90°. Adding them as phasors gives the supply voltage V = I√(R² + X_L²), so Z = √(R² + X_L²) and the current lags the voltage by φ = tan⁻¹(X_L/R), somewhere between 0° (pure R) and 90° (pure L). The power factor cos φ = R/Z is lagging. Phasor diagram in words: draw I along the reference axis; V_R lies along I, V_L points straight up, and their resultant V sits at angle φ above I. (Many books write the phase angle as θ instead of φ.)
Series R-C Circuit

Now V_C = IX_C lags I by 90°. The impedance is Z = √(R² + X_C²), the current leads the voltage by φ = tan⁻¹(X_C/R), and the power factor cos φ = R/Z is leading. Phasor diagram: V_R along I, V_C pointing straight down, and the resultant V below I at angle φ.
Series RLC Impedance
Impedance combines resistance and net reactance as a phasor. V_L and V_C are 180° apart, so only the difference X_L − X_C matters. Its magnitude and phase angle are:

concepts.plainText: Z = sqrt(R² + (XL − XC)²); tan(phi) = (XL − XC)/R

concepts.text: Transient Response to DC Switching

When a DC source is switched onto an R-L or R-C circuit the current or voltage does not jump; it follows an exponential curve governed by the time constant τ. R-L circuit: τ = L/R and the current rises as i = (V/R)(1 − e^(−t/τ)). R-C circuit: τ = RC; the capacitor voltage rises as v_C = V(1 − e^(−t/τ)) while the charging current decays as (V/R)e^(−t/τ). In one time constant a rising quantity reaches 63.2 % of its final value (a decaying one falls to 36.8 %), and after 5τ the transient is complete for practical purposes (99.3 %).

concepts.plainText: τ(RL) = L/R; τ(RC) = RC

concepts.text: Going Deeper: R-L, R-C and R-L-C Circuits

Complex (j) notation turns phasor diagrams into ordinary algebra. A resistor has impedance R, an inductor +jX_L and a capacitor −jX_C, so a series circuit has Z = R + j(X_L − X_C). The magnitude |Z| gives the current from I = V/|Z|, and the angle φ = tan⁻¹((X_L − X_C)/R) tells you whether the current lags (positive φ) or leads (negative φ). Multiplying every side of the impedance triangle by I gives the voltage triangle V_R, V_X and V, which is why voltmeter readings in a series circuit never add arithmetically.

concepts.plainText: Z = R + j(XL − XC) = |Z| at angle φ; I = V / |Z|

concepts.text: In a parallel circuit the voltage is common and the branch currents add as phasors. The resistor current I_R = V/R is in phase with V, the inductor current I_L = V/X_L lags by 90° and the capacitor current I_C = V/X_C leads by 90°, so I_L and I_C partly cancel. The total current is √(I_R² + (I_C − I_L)²) and the combined impedance is V divided by that current, always smaller than the smallest branch opposition in an R-L or R-C pair.

concepts.latex: I = \sqrt{I_R^2 + (I_C - I_L)^2}, \qquad Z_{R\parallel X} = \frac{R X}{\sqrt{R^2 + X^2}}
concepts.plainText: I = √(I_R² + (I_C − I_L)²); R in parallel with X: Z = RX / √(R² + X²)

rows: Raising f in an R-L pair

concepts.text: The transient results come from one first-order equation. For an R-L circuit, KVL gives V = Ri + L di/dt, whose solution rising from zero is i = (V/R)(1 − e^(−Rt/L)); the R-C case is identical with v_C in place of i and RC in place of L/R. Two continuity rules fix the starting point: capacitor voltage and inductor current cannot jump. So at t = 0+ an uncharged capacitor acts as a short circuit and an inductor carrying no initial current as an open circuit, while in DC steady state the capacitor is open and the inductor is a short. The time to reach any voltage v on a rising curve follows by taking logarithms.

concepts.plainText: t = τ ln(V / (V − v)); time to 50 % = 0.693 τ

concepts.text:
Example 1: series R = 15 Ω, L = 0.2 H, C = 80 µF on 230 V, 50 Hz
X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.2 = 62.83 Ω
X_C = 1/(2π × 50 × 80×10⁻⁶) = 39.79 Ω
Net X = 62.83 − 39.79 = 23.04 Ω (inductive)
|Z| = √(15² + 23.04²) = 27.50 Ω
I = 230/27.50 = 8.37 A, lagging by φ = tan⁻¹(23.04/15) = 56.9°
Power factor = cos φ = 15/27.50 = 0.546 lagging
V_R = 125.5 V, V_L = 525.6 V, V_C = 332.8 V
Note V_L = 526 V exceeds the 230 V supply; check √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²) = 230 V

Example 2: R = 47 kΩ, C = 22 µF (uncharged) switched onto 12 V DC
τ = RC = 47×10³ × 22×10⁻⁶ = 1.034 s
Initial current i(0+) = V/R = 12/47 kΩ = 0.255 mA (capacitor acts as a short)
At t = 1 s: v_C = 12(1 − e^(−1/1.034)) = 7.44 V
Time to reach 9 V: t = τ ln(12/(12 − 9)) = 1.034 × ln 4 = 1.43 s
Practically fully charged after 5τ = 5.2 s
Common mistakes and how to avoid them:
items: Adding V_R + V_L + V_C, or R + X, arithmetically; use the square root of squares because they are 90° apart.
Forgetting to convert mH to H and µF to F before using 2πfL or 1/(2πfC).
Assuming X_L > X_C always means lagging current; that is true in series, but in parallel the larger current flows in the smaller reactance, so X_L > X_C makes a parallel circuit capacitive.
Using τ = R/L or τ = RL for an R-L circuit; the correct time constant is L/R.
Treating a capacitor as an open circuit at the switching instant; it is a short at t = 0+ and an open circuit only in DC steady state.

concepts.text: For any series circuit question, write X_L, X_C, net X, |Z|, I and φ in that order before looking at the options. Most wrong options come from skipping the net-reactance step or from adding R and X directly.

formulas.plainText: tan φ = (XL − XC)/R; power factor cos φ = R/Z
τ = L/R for R-L; τ = RC for R-C

notes.text: Check units before computing: f in Hz, L in henries, C in farads. Convert mH and µF first; unit slips are the number one cause of wrong options that LOOK right.
Impedances add as phasors, not arithmetically: R and X are at right angles, hence the square root of squares. Z = R + X_L is never correct.

One time constant: 63.2 % of the final value reached on a rising curve, 36.8 % left on a falling one. Five time constants: steady state (99.3 %). Both R-L and R-C use the same 63.2 % rule; only τ differs.

flashcards.back: X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.1 = 31.4 Ω; I = 230/31.4 ≈ 7.3 A, lagging the voltage by 90°.

flashcards.front: What does the mnemonic CIVIL tell you?
flashcards.back: In a Capacitor, I leads V; V leads I in an inductor (L).

flashcards.front: What fraction of the final value is reached after one time constant?
