flashcards.front: A series circuit has R = 6 Ω and X_L = 8 Ω. Find Z, φ and the power factor.

questions.questionText: What is the reactance of a 50 mH inductor at 50 Hz?
questions.explanation: X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 0.05 = 15.71 Ω. Using 50 instead of 0.05 H gives 15708 Ω, a unit slip.

questions.questionText: A 10 µF capacitor is connected to a 50 Hz supply. Its capacitive reactance is:
questions.explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 50 × 10×10⁻⁶) = 318.3 Ω. 0.00314 Ω is 2πfC, the reciprocal mistake.

questions.questionText: If the supply frequency applied to a capacitor is doubled, its capacitive reactance:
questions.explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC) is inversely proportional to frequency, so doubling f halves X_C.

questions.questionText: The reciprocal of the impedance of an AC circuit is called its:
questions.explanation: Y = 1/Z = G + jB, measured in siemens; its real part is the conductance G and its imaginary part is the susceptance B. Admittances of parallel branches add directly.

questions.questionText: A capacitor charges from 0 V through a resistor from a DC source. What percentage of the final voltage has it reached after one time constant?
questions.explanation: v_C/V = 1 − e^(−1) = 1 − 0.368 = 0.632, i.e. 63.2 %. 36.8 % is what remains of a decaying quantity, and 86.5 % is reached after 2τ.

questions.questionText: What is the time constant of a series circuit with R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 µF?
A coil of inductance 0.5 H and resistance 10 Ω is switched onto a DC supply. What is its time constant?
questions.explanation: τ = L/R = 0.5/10 = 0.05 s = 50 ms. 5 s is L × R and 20 s is R/L.

questions.questionText: In the phasor diagram of a series R-L circuit, the voltage across the resistor is:
options: 180° out of phase with the current
questions.explanation: A resistor's voltage V_R = IR is always in phase with its current; only the inductor voltage leads the current by 90°.

questions.questionText: Which quantity is the same for every element of a series R-L-C circuit?
questions.explanation: Series elements carry the same current; their voltages differ in size and phase. In a parallel circuit it is the voltage that is common.

questions.questionText: A series circuit has R = 5 Ω and X_C = 12 Ω. What is the magnitude of its impedance?
questions.explanation: |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 Ω. 17 Ω is the arithmetic sum, a common error.

questions.questionText: In a series R-L circuit the voltmeter readings are V_R = 30 V and V_L = 40 V. What is the supply voltage?
questions.explanation: V_R and V_L are 90° apart, so V = √(30² + 40²) = 50 V, not the arithmetic sum of 70 V.

questions.questionText: What is the smallest whole number of time constants after which an R-C or R-L transient has completed more than 99 % of its total change?
questions.explanation: 1 − e^(−n): 3τ gives 95.0 %, 4τ gives 98.2 % and 5τ gives 99.3 %, so five time constants are needed.

questions.questionText: A series circuit of R = 40 Ω and L = 0.1 H is connected to 230 V, 50 Hz. What current flows?
A series R-C circuit has R = 10 Ω and X_C = 10 Ω. The phase angle between the supply voltage and the current is:
questions.explanation: tan φ = X_C/R = 10/10 = 1, so φ = 45°. In an R-C circuit the current leads the voltage.

questions.questionText: A series R-C circuit has R = 24 Ω and X_C = 7 Ω. Its power factor is:
questions.explanation: |Z| = √(24² + 7²) = 25 Ω and pf = R/|Z| = 24/25 = 0.96, leading because the circuit is capacitive. 0.28 is X_C/|Z| (sin φ).

questions.questionText: A series R-L-C circuit has R = 8 Ω, X_L = 20 Ω and X_C = 14 Ω. Its impedance and phase angle are:
questions.explanation: Net X = 20 − 14 = 6 Ω (inductive), |Z| = √(8² + 6²) = 10 Ω and φ = tan⁻¹(6/8) = 36.9°, current lagging.

questions.questionText: In a series R-L-C circuit, V_R = 60 V, V_L = 120 V and V_C = 40 V. What is the supply voltage?
questions.explanation: V = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²) = √(60² + 80²) = 100 V. 220 V is the arithmetic sum.

questions.questionText: In a series R-L-C circuit, X_C is greater than X_L. The circuit behaves as:
options: Capacitive, with the current leading the supply voltage
Inductive, with the current lagging the supply voltage
Purely resistive, with the current in phase
An open circuit, with zero current
questions.explanation: The net reactance X_L − X_C is negative (capacitive), so the current leads the supply voltage by tan⁻¹((X_C − X_L)/R).

questions.questionText: Which statement about a series R-L-C circuit on AC is correct?
options: The supply voltage is the arithmetic sum V_R + V_L + V_C
V_L and V_C are in phase with each other
The current is always in phase with the supply voltage
The voltage across L or C alone can be greater than the supply voltage
questions.explanation: V_L and V_C are 180° apart and partly cancel, so each can exceed the supply voltage while their difference stays small.

questions.questionText: A capacitor charges from 0 V through a resistor from a 10 V DC supply with a time constant of 1 ms. What is the capacitor voltage 2 ms after switching on?
questions.explanation: v_C = V(1 − e^(−t/τ)) = 10(1 − e^(−2)) = 10(1 − 0.135) = 8.65 V. 1.35 V is the remaining difference, not the capacitor voltage.

questions.questionText: A capacitor charged to 100 V discharges through a resistor with a time constant of 2 s. What is its voltage 2 s after discharge begins?
questions.explanation: v = V₀e^(−t/τ) = 100 e^(−1) = 36.8 V. After one time constant a decaying quantity keeps 36.8 % of its initial value.

questions.questionText: A 12 V DC supply is switched onto a coil with R = 4 Ω and L = 2 H. What is the current 0.5 s after switching?
An uncharged capacitor in series with a 5 kΩ resistor is switched onto a 20 V DC supply. What current flows at the instant of switching (t = 0+)?
questions.explanation: An uncharged capacitor cannot change its voltage instantly, so it acts as a short at t = 0+: i = V/R = 20/5000 = 4 mA. The current then decays exponentially.

questions.questionText: At the instant a DC source is switched onto a series R-L circuit whose inductor carries no initial current, the inductor behaves as:
options: A short circuit, so the initial current is V/R
An open circuit, so the initial current is zero
questions.explanation: Inductor current cannot change instantaneously, so it starts at zero; the whole supply voltage appears across L at t = 0+.

questions.questionText: At what frequency does a 20 mH inductor have a reactance of 100 Ω?
questions.explanation: f = X_L/(2πL) = 100/(2π × 0.02) = 795.8 Hz. 5000 is X_L/L, which is ω in rad/s, not f in Hz.

questions.questionText: A 30 Ω resistor and an inductor of reactance 40 Ω are connected in parallel across 120 V AC. What is the total supply current?
questions.explanation: I_R = 120/30 = 4 A and I_L = 120/40 = 3 A, 90° apart, so I = √(4² + 3²) = 5 A. 2.4 A would be the series-circuit answer 120/50.

questions.questionText: A 30 Ω resistor is connected in parallel with a capacitor of reactance 40 Ω. What is the magnitude of the combined impedance?
questions.explanation: |Z| = RX_C/√(R² + X_C²) = 30 × 40/50 = 24 Ω. 17.1 Ω is the product-over-sum formula applied as if both were resistors.

questions.questionText: A resistor and a capacitor are connected in parallel across an AC supply. Which statement is correct?
options: The supply current lags the voltage
The supply current leads the voltage and |Z| is smaller than R
The supply current equals the arithmetic sum of the branch currents
|Z| is larger than both R and X_C
questions.explanation: The capacitor branch current leads V by 90°, pulling the total current ahead of V. Branch currents add as phasors, and a parallel combination is always smaller than either branch.

questions.questionText: A 10 Ω resistor in series with a capacitive reactance of 5 Ω has an impedance, in rectangular form, of:
questions.explanation: Capacitive reactance is written as −jX_C, so Z = 10 − j5 Ω, with magnitude √125 = 11.2 Ω.

questions.questionText: A series R-C circuit with R = 60 Ω and X_C = 80 Ω is connected to 100 V AC. What is the voltage across the capacitor?
questions.explanation: |Z| = √(60² + 80²) = 100 Ω, I = 100/100 = 1 A and V_C = IX_C = 80 V. 57.1 V comes from treating the circuit as a resistive divider.

questions.questionText: Which quantity cannot change instantaneously at a switching instant (finite voltages and currents assumed)?
questions.explanation: Changing v_C instantly would need infinite current (i = C dv/dt). The inductor's current, not its voltage, is the other continuous quantity.

questions.questionText: In a series R-L circuit with fixed R and L, the supply frequency is increased at constant voltage. Which change occurs?
options: The impedance rises, the current falls and the lagging phase angle increases
The impedance falls, the current rises and the phase angle decreases
The impedance and phase angle stay the same
The current begins to lead the voltage
questions.explanation: X_L = 2πfL grows with f, so |Z| = √(R² + X_L²) rises, I = V/|Z| falls and φ = tan⁻¹(X_L/R) increases towards 90° lagging.

questions.questionText: Which statement about reactance is NOT correct?
options: Inductive reactance is proportional to frequency
Capacitive reactance is inversely proportional to frequency
An ideal reactance dissipates average power just as a resistance does
questions.explanation: An ideal inductor or capacitor stores energy for part of each cycle and returns it, so its average power is zero. The other statements are true.

questions.questionText: A series circuit of R = 10 Ω, L = 0.1 H and C = 50 µF is connected to 230 V, 50 Hz. The current and its phase relation to the supply voltage are:
A coil draws 5 A from a 100 V DC supply and 4 A from a 100 V, 50 Hz AC supply. What is its inductance?
questions.explanation: DC gives R = 100/5 = 20 Ω; AC gives |Z| = 100/4 = 25 Ω, so X_L = √(25² − 20²) = 15 Ω and L = 15/(2π × 50) = 47.7 mH. 79.6 mH wrongly uses |Z| as X_L.

questions.questionText: A 1 µF capacitor, initially uncharged, charges through a 1 MΩ resistor from a 10 V DC supply. How long does it take to reach 5 V?
questions.explanation: τ = RC = 10⁶ × 10⁻⁶ = 1 s. From 5 = 10(1 − e^(−t/τ)), e^(−t) = 0.5 and t = τ ln 2 = 0.693 s. One τ (1 s) would give 6.32 V.

questions.questionText: A 20 V DC supply is switched onto a coil with R = 5 Ω and L = 0.4 H. In steady state, the current and the energy stored in the magnetic field are:
questions.explanation: Steady-state current I = V/R = 20/5 = 4 A (the inductor is a short). Stored energy W = ½LI² = 0.5 × 0.4 × 4² = 3.2 J; 6.4 J forgets the ½.

questions.questionText: A series R-C circuit with R = 40 Ω draws 4 A from a 200 V, 50 Hz supply. What is the capacitance?
A series R-L-C circuit has R = 20 Ω, X_L = 50 Ω and X_C = 35 Ω and carries 4 A. What are the supply voltage and the voltage across the inductor?
questions.explanation: |Z| = √(20² + 15²) = 25 Ω, so V = 4 × 25 = 100 V, while V_L = IX_L = 4 × 50 = 200 V. The inductor voltage exceeds the supply because V_C (140 V) opposes it.

questions.questionText: A 40 Ω resistor, an inductor of reactance 30 Ω and a capacitor of reactance 60 Ω are connected in parallel across 120 V AC. The supply current is:
questions.explanation: I_R = 3 A, I_L = 4 A (lagging), I_C = 2 A (leading); I = √(3² + (4 − 2)²) = √13 = 3.61 A. The inductive branch current is larger, so the total lags.

questions.questionText: A 100 µF capacitor, initially uncharged, is charged through 10 kΩ from a 50 V DC supply. What is the charging current 1 s after switching on?
questions.explanation: τ = RC = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁴ = 1 s and i(0+) = 50/10⁴ = 5 mA, so i = 5e^(−1) = 1.84 mA. 3.16 mA wrongly uses the rising factor (1 − e^(−1)).

questions.questionText: A series R-L circuit has R = 100 Ω and L = 0.1 H. At what supply frequency does the current lag the voltage by exactly 45°?
questions.explanation: φ = 45° requires X_L = R = 100 Ω, so f = R/(2πL) = 100/(2π × 0.1) = 159.2 Hz. 1000 is ω = R/L in rad/s.

subtopics.title: Resonance in AC Circuits
subtopics.subtitle: X_L = X_C: series acceptor, parallel rejector, Q factor and bandwidth

concepts.text: Resonance Condition

Resonance occurs in a circuit containing both L and C at the frequency where the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal, X_L = X_C. Because X_L rises and X_C falls with frequency, there is exactly one such frequency, the resonant frequency f_r. Setting 2πf_rL = 1/(2πf_rC) gives f_r = 1/(2π√LC), which depends only on L and C and not on R.

concepts.plainText: fr = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC))

concepts.text: Series Resonance
A series RLC circuit resonates at the frequency where X_L = X_C. The reactances cancel, impedance drops to R (minimum), and current is maximum and in phase with the voltage.
At series resonance:
items: Z = R (minimum), I = V/R (maximum), phase angle 0°.
Power factor = 1 (unity); the circuit looks purely resistive.
Voltage across L and across C can each exceed the supply (Q times larger): voltage magnification.
Called an acceptor circuit because it accepts (passes) the resonant frequency and rejects others.
Below f_r the circuit is capacitive (current leads); above f_r it is inductive (current lags).

concepts.text: Quality Factor, Bandwidth and Half-Power Frequencies

The quality factor Q measures how sharp (selective) the resonance is: Q = X_L/R = X_C/R = (1/R)√(L/C), evaluated at f_r. It also equals the voltage magnification V_L/V = V_C/V at resonance. The bandwidth BW = f₂ − f₁ is the range between the two half-power (cut-off) frequencies at which the current falls to 1/√2 (70.7 %) of its maximum and the power to half; there Z = √2 R and the phase angle is ±45°. Since BW = f_r/Q = R/(2πL), a high Q means a narrow bandwidth.

concepts.plainText: Q = XL/R = (1/R) sqrt(L/C) = fr/BW
BW = f2 − f1 = fr/Q = R/(2 pi L)

concepts.text: Parallel Resonance

Parallel resonance is the dual: impedance is maximum (ideally infinite for lossless L and C), the line current is minimum and in phase with the supply, so it is a rejector circuit that blocks the resonant frequency. The branch currents in L and C are each Q times the line current (current magnification) and cancel each other. For a practical coil of resistance R in parallel with C, the impedance at resonance is the dynamic impedance Z_r = L/(CR), purely resistive. Used in tuning circuits (radio, TV) and as the tank circuit of LC oscillators.

concepts.plainText: Dynamic impedance at parallel resonance: Zr = L/(CR)

rows: Rejector; band-stop filter, tank circuit of oscillators

concepts.text: Worked Example

A series circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 100 mH and C = 10 µF and is fed from 100 V. LC = 0.1 × 10 × 10⁻⁶ = 10⁻⁶, so f_r = 1/(2π × 10⁻³) = 159.2 Hz. At resonance I = 100/10 = 10 A; X_L = 2π × 159.2 × 0.1 = 100 Ω, so Q = 100/10 = 10 (also (1/10)√(0.1/10⁻⁵) = 10); V_L = V_C = 10 × 100 = 1000 V, ten times the supply; BW = f_r/Q = 15.9 Hz, so the half-power frequencies are roughly 151 Hz and 167 Hz.
Going Deeper: Resonance

The half-power frequencies come from setting the net reactance equal to R, so that |Z| = √2 R. For a series circuit this gives ωL − 1/(ωC) = ±R, a quadratic in ω whose two positive roots are ω₁ and ω₂. Subtracting the two equations shows ω₂ − ω₁ = R/L exactly, which is why BW = R/(2πL) holds for any Q. Multiplying them shows ω₁ω₂ = 1/(LC) = ω₀², so the resonant frequency is the geometric mean of f₁ and f₂, and the curve is only symmetric about f_r when Q is high (about 10 or more).

concepts.plainText: fr = √(f1 f2); Q = 2π × energy stored / energy lost per cycle

concepts.text: At resonance energy swings back and forth between the magnetic field of L and the electric field of C, and the total stored energy stays constant at ½ L I_m² = ½ C V_Cm². The source only has to replace the energy burnt in R, which is I²R per second. The ratio of stored energy to energy lost per cycle, multiplied by 2π, is the general definition of Q; for a series circuit it reduces to ω₀L/R, and it also equals the ratio of the reactive power in L (or C) to the active power in R.

A practical tank circuit is a coil (L in series with its resistance R) in parallel with C. Making the admittance purely real gives a resonant frequency slightly below the ideal value, and resonance exists only if R < √(L/C). At that frequency the impedance is L/(CR) = Q²R, where Q = ω₀L/R is the coil Q. For the ideal three-branch parallel RLC circuit the roles of R are reversed: Q = R√(C/L) and BW = 1/(2πRC), so a larger parallel resistance gives a sharper response.

concepts.plainText: Coil in parallel with C: fr = (1/2π)√(1/(LC) − R²/L²)

rows: Lower coil Q, lower Z_r, wider BW
Current in L and C branches

concepts.text:
Example 2: coil L = 500 µH, R = 25 Ω, in parallel with C = 500 pF, V = 10 V
Ideal f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π × 5 × 10⁻⁷) = 318.3 kHz
R²/L² = 2.5 × 10⁹, tiny beside 1/(LC) = 4 × 10¹², so f_r ≈ 318.2 kHz
Q = ω0 L / R = (2 × 10⁶ × 5 × 10⁻⁴)/25 = 40
Z_r = L/(CR) = 5 × 10⁻⁴/(5 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 25) = 40 kΩ (= Q²R)
Line current = 10 V / 40 kΩ = 0.25 mA
Capacitor current ≈ V ω0 C = 10 × 2 × 10⁶ × 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 10 mA = Q × 0.25 mA
Common mistakes:
items: Using BW = R/L and calling it hertz: R/L is the bandwidth in rad/s; divide by 2π for Hz.
Taking f_r as the arithmetic mean of f₁ and f₂; it is the geometric mean, and the difference matters when Q is low.
Applying the series formulas Q = (1/R)√(L/C) and BW = R/(2πL) to a three-branch parallel circuit, where Q = R√(C/L).
Forgetting that a parallel circuit is inductive below f_r and capacitive above it, the reverse of a series circuit.
Using rms current in ½ L I² when the peak stored energy is asked for.

concepts.text: Quick checks: at f_r, X_L = X_C = √(L/C); Q (series) = √(L/C)/R; BW = f_r/Q. If an answer for f_r changes when only R changes (series circuit), a formula has been misapplied.

formulas.plainText: BW = f2 − f1 = R/(2 pi L)

formulas.latex: V_L = V_C = Q V \quad \text{(series, at } f_r)
formulas.plainText: At series resonance: V_L = V_C = Q × V
Parallel resonance dynamic impedance: Zr = L/(CR)

notes.text: Series resonance: minimum Z, maximum I. Parallel resonance: maximum Z, minimum I. Swapping these is the most common trap.
f_r depends only on L and C. Changing R alters Q, the bandwidth and the peak current, but never the resonant frequency of a series circuit.
At the half-power frequencies the current is 0.707 I_max, not 0.5 I_max: power is halved because it goes as I². The impedance there is √2 R.

formulas.title: Resonant frequency
formulas.description: Frequency at which X_L = X_C for any L-C combination; L in henry, C in farad, f in hertz.

formulas.title: Quality factor
formulas.description: Sharpness of a series resonance and the voltage magnification across L or C at f_r.

formulas.title: Bandwidth
formulas.description: Width between the half-power frequencies where current is 70.7 % of maximum; narrower for higher Q.

formulas.title: Voltage magnification
formulas.description: Voltage across the inductor or capacitor of a series circuit at resonance; can be many times the supply voltage.

formulas.title: Dynamic impedance (parallel resonance)
formulas.description: Purely resistive impedance of a coil (L with series resistance R) in parallel with C at resonance; the line current is V/Z_r.

flashcards.front: L = 1 mH and C = 1 µF. What is the resonant frequency?
Why is a series resonant circuit called an acceptor?
flashcards.back: At f_r its impedance falls to R, so it passes (accepts) current at the resonant frequency and opposes other frequencies.

flashcards.front: A series circuit has f_r = 1 MHz and Q = 50. Find the bandwidth and the half-power frequencies.
flashcards.back: BW = f_r/Q = 20 kHz; f₁ ≈ 990 kHz and f₂ ≈ 1010 kHz.

flashcards.front: What happens to Q, bandwidth and f_r if R is doubled in a series RLC circuit?
flashcards.back: Q halves (Q = X_L/R), the bandwidth doubles, and f_r is unchanged because it depends only on L and C.

questions.questionText: A series circuit has L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF. Its resonant frequency is approximately:
questions.explanation: f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π√(10⁻² × 10⁻⁶)) = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1592 Hz ≈ 1.59 kHz. Leaving out 2π gives 10 kHz; leaving out the square root gives 15.9 MHz.

questions.questionText: Below its resonant frequency, a series RLC circuit behaves as:
options: An inductive circuit, with current lagging the voltage
A purely resistive circuit, with current in phase with the voltage
A capacitive circuit, with current leading the voltage
A capacitive circuit, with current lagging the voltage
questions.explanation: Below f_r, X_C = 1/(ωC) is larger than X_L = ωL, so the net reactance is capacitive and the current leads the voltage.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 20 Ω is at resonance, where X_L = X_C = 50 Ω. With a 100 V supply, the current is:
questions.explanation: At resonance the reactances cancel, so Z = R = 20 Ω and I = V/R = 100/20 = 5 A.

questions.questionText: In a series RLC circuit, the impedance at each half-power frequency is equal to:
questions.explanation: At a half-power frequency the current is I_max/√2, so the impedance is √2 times its minimum value R; there |X_L − X_C| = R.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 0.4 H and C = 10 µF. Its quality factor is:
A parallel resonant circuit is also known as a:
questions.explanation: At parallel resonance the impedance is maximum and the line current minimum, so the circuit rejects (blocks) the resonant frequency.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit has R = 20 Ω and L = 0.1 H. Its bandwidth is approximately:
questions.explanation: BW = R/(2πL) = 20/(2π × 0.1) ≈ 31.8 Hz. R/L = 200 is the bandwidth in rad/s, not in Hz.

questions.questionText: A series resonant circuit has f_r = 10 kHz and Q = 50. Its bandwidth is:
The quality factor Q of a resonant circuit is measured in:
options: No unit; it is a dimensionless ratio
questions.explanation: Q is a ratio of like quantities (reactance to resistance, or energy stored to energy lost), so it has no unit.

questions.questionText: A series circuit with R = 10 Ω, L = 50 mH and C = 0.5 µF is connected to a 10 V supply at its resonant frequency. The voltage across the inductor is approximately:
questions.explanation: At resonance X_L = √(L/C) = √(0.05/(0.5 × 10⁻⁶)) ≈ 316 Ω and I = V/R = 1 A, so V_L = I X_L ≈ 316 V (Q ≈ 31.6 times the supply).

questions.questionText: In a series RLC circuit, R is increased while L and C are kept constant. Which quantity remains unchanged?
questions.explanation: f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) does not contain R. Raising R lowers Q and the peak current and widens the bandwidth.

questions.questionText: Current magnification occurs in:
options: A series resonant circuit, where the line current is Q times V/R
A series resonant circuit, where the current in L is Q times the current in C
Any RC circuit driven above its corner frequency
A parallel resonant circuit, where each branch current can be Q times the line current
questions.explanation: In a parallel resonant circuit the L and C branch currents are nearly equal and opposite, each about Q times the small line current. Series resonance gives voltage magnification instead.

questions.questionText: A resonant circuit with a higher Q has:
options: A wider bandwidth and higher selectivity
A narrower bandwidth and lower selectivity
A narrower bandwidth and higher selectivity
A higher resonant frequency with the same bandwidth
questions.explanation: BW = f_r/Q, so a higher Q gives a narrower bandwidth, which means the circuit discriminates more sharply between nearby frequencies (higher selectivity).

questions.questionText: A series LC circuit resonates at 1 kHz. If the capacitance is made four times larger with L unchanged, the new resonant frequency is:
questions.explanation: f_r ∝ 1/√C, so multiplying C by 4 divides f_r by √4 = 2: 1000/2 = 500 Hz.

questions.questionText: What capacitance must be placed in series with a 0.5 H inductor to give resonance at 50 Hz?
A 253 pF capacitor is to resonate at 1 MHz. The inductance required is approximately:
A series resonant circuit has f_r = 455 kHz and Q = 50. Its half-power frequencies are approximately:
questions.explanation: BW = f_r/Q = 455/50 = 9.1 kHz. For a high-Q circuit f₁ ≈ f_r − BW/2 = 450.45 kHz and f₂ ≈ f_r + BW/2 = 459.55 kHz.

questions.questionText: The half-power frequencies of a series RLC circuit are 40 kHz and 90 kHz. The resonant frequency and the quality factor are:
questions.explanation: For a series RLC circuit f_r is the geometric mean: f_r = √(f₁f₂) = √(40 × 90) = 60 kHz. BW = 50 kHz, so Q = f_r/BW = 60/50 = 1.2. The arithmetic mean (65 kHz) is only an approximation for high Q.

questions.questionText: A coil of inductance 0.2 H and resistance 20 Ω is connected in parallel with a 10 µF capacitor across a 200 V supply at the resonant frequency. The line current is:
questions.explanation: Dynamic impedance Z_r = L/(CR) = 0.2/(10⁻⁵ × 20) = 1000 Ω, so the line current is 200/1000 = 0.2 A.

questions.questionText: A coil with L = 0.1 H and R = 60 Ω is connected in parallel with a 10 µF capacitor. The resonant frequency of the combination is approximately:
questions.explanation: f_r = (1/2π)√(1/(LC) − R²/L²) = (1/2π)√(10⁶ − 3.6 × 10⁵) = 800/(2π) ≈ 127 Hz, lower than the ideal value 1/(2π√(LC)) ≈ 159 Hz because of the coil resistance.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 0.1 H and C = 10 µF. When it is supplied at twice its resonant frequency, its impedance and nature are:
questions.explanation: At f_r, X_L = X_C = √(L/C) = 100 Ω. At 2f_r, X_L = 200 Ω and X_C = 50 Ω, so Z = √(10² + 150²) ≈ 150 Ω; X_L > X_C, so the circuit is inductive.

questions.questionText: An ideal parallel RLC circuit (R, L and C each in a separate branch) has R = 10 kΩ, L = 1 mH and C = 10 nF. Its quality factor and bandwidth are:
questions.explanation: For the three-branch parallel circuit Q = R√(C/L) = 10⁴ × √(10⁻⁵) ≈ 31.6 and BW = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1.59 kHz. The series formulas (1/R)√(L/C) and R/(2πL) do not apply here.

questions.questionText: A coil of inductance 2 mH and resistance 25 Ω is used at 100 kHz. Its quality factor at this frequency is approximately:
In terms of energy, the quality factor of a resonant circuit is defined as:
options: (maximum energy stored) / (2π × energy dissipated per cycle)
questions.explanation: Q = 2π × W_stored/W_lost per cycle. For a series circuit this reduces to ω₀L/R, the familiar X_L/R.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 50 Ω is fed from a 100 V variable-frequency supply. The power dissipated at either half-power frequency is:
questions.explanation: Maximum power at resonance is V²/R = 100²/50 = 200 W. At a half-power frequency it is half of this, 100 W.

questions.questionText: The maximum current of a series RLC circuit at resonance is 4 A. The current at the lower half-power frequency is approximately:
questions.explanation: At a half-power frequency I = I_max/√2 = 4 × 0.707 ≈ 2.83 A, which makes the power I²R exactly half the maximum.

questions.questionText: At the upper half-power frequency of a series RLC circuit, the current:
options: Is in phase with the supply voltage
questions.explanation: Above f_r the circuit is inductive, and at f₂ the net reactance X_L − X_C equals R, so tan φ = 1 and the current lags by 45°.

questions.questionText: At series resonance, the net voltage across the series L-C combination (measured across both together) is:
options: Zero, because V_L and V_C are equal and 180° apart
questions.explanation: V_L and V_C are each Q × V but in antiphase, so their phasor sum is zero and the whole supply voltage appears across R.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 5 Ω resonates at 1 kHz. With 10 V applied at resonance, the voltage across the capacitor is 250 V. The inductance is approximately:
questions.explanation: I = V/R = 10/5 = 2 A, so X_C = V_C/I = 125 Ω. At resonance X_L = X_C = 125 Ω, so L = 125/(2π × 1000) ≈ 19.9 mH (Q = 25).

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit must resonate at 10 kHz with a bandwidth of 100 Hz using a 10 mH inductor. The required R and C are approximately:
A radio tuning circuit uses a fixed inductor with a variable capacitor adjustable from 30 pF to 300 pF. The ratio of the highest to the lowest resonant frequency is approximately:
A tuned circuit with a fixed inductor must cover 550 kHz to 1650 kHz. The ratio C_max/C_min of the variable capacitor must be:
questions.explanation: C ∝ 1/f², so C_max/C_min = (f_max/f_min)² = (1650/550)² = 3² = 9.

questions.questionText: A parallel tank circuit with Q = 40 draws a line current of 5 mA at resonance. The current in the capacitor branch is approximately:
questions.explanation: At parallel resonance each branch current is about Q times the line current: I_C ≈ 40 × 5 mA = 200 mA.

questions.questionText: A coil (L = 200 µH, R = 10 Ω) is connected in parallel with a 200 pF capacitor. Its resonant frequency and dynamic impedance are approximately:
questions.explanation: Since R² ≪ L/C, f_r ≈ 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π × 2 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 796 kHz. Z_r = L/(CR) = 200 × 10⁻⁶/(200 × 10⁻¹² × 10) = 100 kΩ (equivalently Q²R with Q = 100). 5 MHz is ω₀ in rad/s, not f.

questions.questionText: Which statement about series resonance is NOT correct?
options: The current is in phase with the supply voltage
Increasing R raises the resonant frequency
The voltages across L and C can each exceed the supply voltage
questions.explanation: f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) is independent of R. The other statements are all true at series resonance.

questions.questionText: In an ideal (lossless) parallel LC circuit at resonance:
options: The line current is zero although the branch currents are not
The branch currents are both zero
questions.explanation: The inductor and capacitor currents are equal in magnitude and 180° apart, so they cancel at the junction; the impedance is infinite and no current is drawn from the supply.

questions.questionText: A wave trap is used to block one interfering frequency from reaching a receiver. It is:
options: A series LC circuit tuned to the unwanted frequency, connected in series with the signal path
A parallel LC circuit tuned to the unwanted frequency, connected in series with the signal path
A parallel LC circuit tuned to the unwanted frequency, connected across the signal path
A resistor connected in series with the signal path
questions.explanation: A parallel resonant circuit has maximum impedance at its resonant frequency, so placed in series with the line it blocks that frequency while passing others.

questions.questionText: An ideal parallel LC circuit is operated above its resonant frequency. It behaves as:
options: An inductive load, because X_L is larger than X_C
A capacitive load, because the capacitor branch draws the larger current
An inductive load, because the inductor branch draws the larger current
questions.explanation: Above f_r, X_C is smaller than X_L, so the capacitor branch current dominates and the net line current leads: the parallel circuit looks capacitive (the opposite of a series circuit).

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 10 Ω has a bandwidth of 50 Hz. If R is increased to 25 Ω with L and C unchanged, the new bandwidth is:
questions.explanation: BW = R/(2πL) is proportional to R: 50 × (25/10) = 125 Hz.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 10 Ω and L = 20 mH is supplied with 20 V (rms) at its resonant frequency. The maximum energy stored in the inductor is:
questions.explanation: I = V/R = 2 A rms, so I_m = 2√2 A. W = ½ L I_m² = ½ × 0.02 × 8 = 0.08 J. Using the rms current gives 0.04 J.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit has R = 100 Ω, L = 0.1 H and C = 10 µF. Its exact upper half-power frequency is approximately:
questions.explanation: ω₂ = R/(2L) + √((R/2L)² + 1/(LC)) = 500 + √(250 000 + 10⁶) ≈ 1618 rad/s, so f₂ ≈ 257.5 Hz. Q = 1 here, so f_r + BW/2 ≈ 238.7 Hz is not accurate.

questions.questionText: A resonant circuit has f_r = 2 MHz and a bandwidth of 40 kHz. Its quality factor is:
A practical coil (L with series resistance R) is connected in parallel with a capacitor C. Resonance (unity power factor) is possible only if:
options: R has any value, because the resonant frequency does not depend on R
questions.explanation: f_r = (1/2π)√(1/(LC) − R²/L²) is real only when 1/(LC) > R²/L², that is R < √(L/C).

subtopics.title: Active and Reactive Power
subtopics.subtitle: P, Q, S, the power triangle, power factor and its correction with capacitors

concepts.text: Instantaneous Power

With v = V_m sin ωt and i = I_m sin(ωt − φ), the instantaneous power is p = vi = VI cos φ − VI cos(2ωt − φ), where V and I are rms values. It pulsates at twice the supply frequency about the constant term VI cos φ, which is the average (active) power actually converted into heat, light or mechanical work. The oscillating part averages to zero over a cycle and represents energy shuttling back and forth between the source and the magnetic or electric fields of L and C.
The Power Triangle

In AC circuits three powers coexist: active power P (watts) does real work, reactive power Q (VAR) oscillates in and out of fields, and apparent power S (VA) is the phasor total. Drawn as a right-angled triangle, P is the base, Q the vertical side and S the hypotenuse; the angle between S and P is the phase angle φ between voltage and current.

concepts.latex: P = VI\cos\phi,\quad Q = VI\sin\phi,\quad S = VI = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2}
concepts.plainText: P = VI cos phi; Q = VI sin phi; S = VI = sqrt(P² + Q²)

concepts.text: The three powers:
items: Real (active) power P = VI cos φ, unit watt (W): the actual power consumed; read by a wattmeter; P = I²R.
Reactive power Q = VI sin φ, unit volt-ampere reactive (VAR): oscillates between source and load and does no net work; Q = I²X.
Apparent power S = VI, unit volt-ampere (VA): the total power the source must supply; transformers and alternators are rated in kVA.
Power triangle: S² = P² + Q², so S = √(P² + Q²); also P = S cos φ and Q = S sin φ.

concepts.text: Power Factor

Power factor pf = cos φ = P/S = R/Z is the fraction of the apparent power that does real work, where φ is the angle between voltage and current. In practical units pf = kW/kVA. It ranges from 0 to 1 and is described as lagging or leading according to whether the current lags or leads the voltage.
Power factor cos φ:
items: Unity for a pure resistance; zero for a pure L or a pure C.
Lagging for inductive loads (motors, transformers, fluorescent-lamp chokes); leading for capacitive loads (capacitor banks, synchronous condensers).
Low power factor means larger current for the same real power; capacitor banks are added in parallel to improve it.

concepts.text: Why a low power factor is bad:
items: For fixed P and V the current is I = P/(V cos φ): a lower pf means a larger current.
Conductors, switchgear, transformers and alternators must be rated for more kVA to deliver the same kW.
Higher I²R copper losses and a larger voltage drop in lines, so poorer voltage regulation.
Utilities charge a penalty when the consumer's pf falls below about 0.8 to 0.9.

concepts.text: Power-Factor Correction

A capacitor connected in parallel with an inductive load supplies leading reactive power Q_C that cancels part of the lagging Q of the load; P is unchanged, so S and the line current fall and φ shrinks. To raise the power factor from cos φ₁ to cos φ₂ the capacitor must supply Q_C = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂) VAR, and its capacitance follows from Q_C = V²/X_C = 2πfCV².

concepts.plainText: Q_C = P (tan φ1 − tan φ2); C = Q_C / (2 pi f V²)

concepts.text: Worked Example

A 230 V, 50 Hz single-phase motor draws 10 A at 0.7 power factor lagging. S = 230 × 10 = 2300 VA; P = 2300 × 0.7 = 1610 W; Q = √(2300² − 1610²) = 1643 VAR lagging. To raise the pf to 0.95: tan φ₁ = 1.020 and tan φ₂ = 0.329, so Q_C = 1610 × (1.020 − 0.329) = 1113 VAR and C = 1113/(2π × 50 × 230²) = 67 µF. The new apparent power is S = 1610/0.95 = 1695 VA and the line current falls from 10 A to 1695/230 = 7.4 A while the motor still receives 1610 W.
Going Deeper: Power in AC Circuits

Multiplying v = √2 V sin ωt by i = √2 I sin(ωt − φ) and using 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B) gives the expression below. The first term is constant; the second oscillates at 2ω and averages to zero over a cycle, so the average power is VI cos φ. Whenever φ is not zero, p goes negative for part of each cycle, which is the moment the inductor or capacitor hands stored energy back to the source.

concepts.plainText: p(t) = VI cos φ − VI cos(2ωt − φ)

concepts.text: Complex power combines all three powers in one phasor: S = V I*, where I* is the conjugate of the current phasor. Its real part is P and its imaginary part is Q, with Q positive for an inductive load and negative for a capacitive one. The conjugate is essential; multiplying V by I directly gives the wrong angle. In terms of the load elements, P = I²R = V_R²/R and Q = I²X = V_X²/X.

concepts.latex: S = V I^{*} = P + jQ, \qquad |S| = VI
concepts.plainText: S = V × conj(I) = P + jQ; |S| = VI

concepts.text: When several loads share a supply, complex power is conserved: the total P is the sum of the individual P values and the total Q is the algebraic sum of the Q values, with capacitive VAR counted as negative. The individual kVA figures do not simply add unless all loads have the same power factor. This is the basis of every power-factor correction calculation: the capacitor adds negative Q while leaving P untouched.

concepts.plainText: Line loss ratio = (cos φ1 / cos φ2)², for the same P and V

concepts.text:
Example 1: 230 V supply; heater 2 kW (pf 1) + motor 3 kW at 0.75 lagging
Motor: tan φ = tan(cos⁻¹ 0.75) = 0.882, Q = 3 × 0.882 = 2.65 kVAR
Total P = 2 + 3 = 5 kW
Total Q = 0 + 2.65 = 2.65 kVAR (lagging)
S = √(5² + 2.65²) = 5.66 kVA (not 2 + 4 = 6 kVA)
Overall pf = 5/5.66 = 0.884 lagging
Line current = 5660/230 = 24.6 A

Example 2: 40 kW, 400 V, 50 Hz single-phase load, pf 0.7 -> 0.95 lagging
tan φ1 = tan(cos⁻¹ 0.7) = 1.020, tan φ2 = tan(cos⁻¹ 0.95) = 0.329
Q_C = 40 × (1.020 − 0.329) = 27.7 kVAR
C = Q_C/(2πfV²) = 27 660/(2π × 50 × 400²) = 550 µF
Current before = 40 000/(400 × 0.7) = 142.9 A
Current after = 40 000/(400 × 0.95) = 105.3 A
Active power stays 40 kW; only Q and S change
Common mistakes:
items: Taking V × I as the power in watts; it is the apparent power in VA unless the pf is 1.
Adding kVA values of different loads arithmetically instead of adding P and Q separately.
Using peak values in VI cos φ: with V_m and I_m the average power is (V_m I_m/2) cos φ.
Forgetting that a capacitor's VAR output is 2πfCV², so it falls with the square of the voltage.
Over-sizing the correction bank so the net Q goes negative and the pf becomes leading.

concepts.text: Keep these tan φ values ready for correction problems: pf 0.9 -> 0.484, 0.866 -> 0.577, 0.8 -> 0.75, 0.707 -> 1.0, 0.6 -> 1.333. Then Q = P tan φ and Q_C = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂) take seconds.

formulas.plainText: P = V I cos φ, watts
Q = V I sin φ, volt-amperes reactive
S = V I = sqrt(P² + Q²), volt-amperes
Capacitor VAR for pf correction: Q_C = P (tan φ1 − tan φ2)

notes.text: Given P and S, power factor is simply P/S. Given R and Z, it is R/Z. Both forms appear in board exams.
Reactive power is not 'lost' (its average is zero), but the extra current it demands causes real I²R losses and voltage drops in the supply lines. That is why utilities penalise a low power factor.

Sign convention: inductive Q is positive (absorbed, lagging pf) and capacitive Q is negative (supplied, leading pf). A capacitor 'generates' the reactive power that an inductor 'consumes', which is the whole basis of pf correction.

formulas.title: Active power
formulas.description: Real power in watts consumed by the load; V and I are rms values and φ the angle between them.

formulas.title: Reactive power
formulas.description: Power in VAR exchanged with the fields of L and C; positive (lagging) for inductive, negative (leading) for capacitive loads.

formulas.title: Apparent power and power triangle
formulas.description: Total power in VA that the source must supply; the hypotenuse of the power triangle.

formulas.title: Power factor
formulas.description: Ratio of active to apparent power (or of resistance to impedance); 1 for pure R, 0 for pure L or C.

formulas.title: Capacitor for power-factor correction
formulas.plainText: Q_C = P (tan φ1 − tan φ2); C = Q_C / (2πfV²)
formulas.description: Reactive power and capacitance of the parallel capacitor that raises the pf from cos φ1 to cos φ2 at supply voltage V and frequency f.

flashcards.front: A load has P = 3 kW and Q = 4 kVAR (inductive). Find S and the power factor.
flashcards.back: S = √(3² + 4²) = 5 kVA; pf = P/S = 3/5 = 0.6 lagging.

flashcards.front: Which instrument reads P, and in which unit are transformers rated?
flashcards.back: A wattmeter reads active power in W (kW); transformers and alternators are rated in apparent power, VA (kVA), because their losses depend on total current.

flashcards.front: How does a parallel capacitor improve the power factor?
flashcards.back: It supplies leading VAR that cancel the load's lagging VAR; P stays the same, S and the line current fall, and φ shrinks.

flashcards.front: A 230 V load draws 5 A at 0.8 pf lagging. Find P, Q and S.

questions.questionText: Apparent power in an AC circuit is expressed in:
questions.explanation: Apparent power S = VI is the product of rms voltage and rms current, measured in VA (or kVA).

questions.questionText: A 200 V supply delivers 5 A to a load at a power factor of 0.6. The active power is:
questions.explanation: P = VI cos φ = 200 × 5 × 0.6 = 600 W. VI = 1000 VA is the apparent power, and 800 would be VI sin φ (in VAR).

questions.questionText: The instrument that directly measures the active power drawn by an AC load is the:
questions.explanation: A wattmeter responds to the product of voltage, current and the cosine of the angle between them, so it reads VI cos φ directly.

questions.questionText: A load draws an apparent power of 10 kVA and an active power of 6 kW. Its reactive power is:
questions.explanation: Q = √(S² − P²) = √(100 − 36) = 8 kVAR. Subtracting 10 − 6 = 4 or adding 6 + 10 are the usual slips.

questions.questionText: A load takes 12 kW of active power and 5 kVAR of reactive power. The apparent power is:
questions.explanation: S = √(P² + Q²) = √(144 + 25) = 13 kVA. Active and reactive powers are at right angles, so they cannot be added arithmetically.

questions.questionText: An induction motor running on load normally operates at:
questions.explanation: An induction motor needs magnetizing current, so it is an inductive load that draws current lagging the voltage (typically 0.7 to 0.9 lagging at full load).

questions.questionText: For a 50 Hz supply, the instantaneous power drawn by a single-phase load pulsates at:
questions.explanation: p = VI cos φ − VI cos(2ωt − φ), so the power varies at twice the supply frequency: 2 × 50 = 100 Hz.

questions.questionText: A current of 4 A flows through a series circuit with R = 10 Ω and impedance Z = 20 Ω. The active power is:
questions.explanation: Active power is dissipated only in the resistance: P = I²R = 4² × 10 = 160 W. I²Z = 320 is the apparent power in VA.

questions.questionText: A series circuit has R = 12 Ω and X_L = 5 Ω. Its power factor is approximately:
questions.explanation: Z = √(12² + 5²) = 13 Ω, so pf = R/Z = 12/13 ≈ 0.923, lagging because the reactance is inductive. 5/13 = 0.385 is sin φ.

questions.questionText: When a capacitor bank is connected in parallel with an inductive load to improve its power factor, the active power taken by the load:
questions.explanation: The capacitor only supplies reactive power; the load's voltage is unchanged, so it takes the same active power. Only the reactive power, apparent power and line current fall.

questions.questionText: A circuit in which the current leads the applied voltage is said to have:
options: A leading power factor, as in a capacitive load
A lagging power factor, as in a capacitive load
A leading power factor, as in an inductive load
A unity power factor, as in a resistive load
questions.explanation: The power factor is named after the current: when the current leads the voltage the pf is leading, which happens with a net capacitive load.

questions.questionText: Large power transformers and alternators are rated in kVA rather than kW because:
options: Their output is always at unity power factor
Their losses depend on voltage and current, not on the load power factor
kVA is always smaller than kW
questions.explanation: Copper loss depends on current and iron loss on voltage, so heating is set by VA. The manufacturer does not know the load pf, so the machine is rated in kVA.

questions.questionText: A load operates at a power factor of 0.8. Its reactive factor (sin φ) is:
questions.explanation: sin φ = √(1 − cos²φ) = √(1 − 0.64) = 0.6. The reactive factor is Q/S.

questions.questionText: A 230 V load draws 10 A at a power factor of 0.8 lagging. The reactive power is:
questions.explanation: sin φ = 0.6, so Q = VI sin φ = 230 × 10 × 0.6 = 1380 VAR. 1840 is VI cos φ, the active power in W.

questions.questionText: A single-phase load of 11.5 kW is supplied at 230 V with a power factor of 0.5. The line current is:
questions.explanation: I = P/(V cos φ) = 11 500/(230 × 0.5) = 100 A. At unity pf the same power would need only 50 A.

questions.questionText: A series circuit with R = 30 Ω and X_L = 40 Ω is connected to 200 V. The active power consumed is:
questions.explanation: Z = √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω, I = 200/50 = 4 A, P = I²R = 16 × 30 = 480 W. 800 VA is the apparent power and 640 VAR the reactive power.

questions.questionText: A series circuit with R = 8 Ω and X_C = 6 Ω is connected to 100 V. The reactive power is:
questions.explanation: Z = √(8² + 6²) = 10 Ω, I = 10 A, Q = I²X_C = 100 × 6 = 600 VAR. The load is capacitive, so the reactive power is leading (supplied by the load).

questions.questionText: A 50 µF capacitor is connected to a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. The reactive power it supplies is approximately:
What capacitance is needed to supply 5 kVAR at 400 V, 50 Hz?
questions.explanation: C = Q_C/(2πfV²) = 5000/(2π × 50 × 400²) ≈ 99.5 µF. Leaving out 2π gives 625 µF.

questions.questionText: A 4 kW heater (unity pf) and a motor taking 3 kW at 0.6 pf lagging are supplied from the same source. The overall power factor is approximately:
questions.explanation: Motor Q = 3 × tan(cos⁻¹0.6) = 4 kVAR. Total P = 7 kW, Q = 4 kVAR, S = √(49 + 16) ≈ 8.06 kVA, so pf = 7/8.06 ≈ 0.87 lagging. Averaging the pfs (0.8) is wrong.

questions.questionText: A load draws 10 A (rms) from a 100 V (rms) supply with the current lagging by 60°. The minimum value of the instantaneous power is:
questions.explanation: p = VI cos φ − VI cos(2ωt − φ) swings between VI cos φ ± VI. P = 1000 × 0.5 = 500 W, so p_min = 500 − 1000 = −500 W: for part of each cycle energy flows back to the source.

questions.questionText: A wattmeter, voltmeter and ammeter connected to a single-phase load read 1200 W, 240 V and 8 A. The power factor of the load is:
A 100 kW load operates at 0.6 pf lagging. The capacitor kVAR needed to raise the power factor to unity is approximately:
questions.explanation: Q_C = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂) = 100 × (1.333 − 0) ≈ 133 kVAR. 167 kVA is the apparent power, and 80 kVAR (P sin φ) is not the load's reactive power.

questions.questionText: A 50 kW load has a power factor of 0.8 lagging. The capacitor kVAR required to improve the power factor to 0.95 lagging is approximately:
questions.explanation: tan φ₁ = 0.75 and tan φ₂ = tan(cos⁻¹0.95) ≈ 0.329, so Q_C = 50 × (0.75 − 0.329) ≈ 21.1 kVAR. 37.5 kVAR is the load's whole reactive power.

questions.questionText: For a fixed active power and supply voltage, the power factor of a load is improved from 0.6 to 0.9. The I²R loss in the supply cable falls to about what fraction of its original value?
questions.explanation: I ∝ 1/cos φ, so loss ∝ 1/cos²φ. New/old = (0.6/0.9)² = 0.444, about 44 %. 67 % is the ratio of the currents, not the losses.

questions.questionText: The voltage and current of a load are V = 100∠30° V and I = 5∠−15° A (rms). The active and reactive powers are approximately:
questions.explanation: S = V I* = (100∠30°)(5∠+15°) = 500∠45° VA = 354 + j354. Positive Q means an inductive (lagging) load; the current lags the voltage by 45°. Using I instead of I* gives the wrong angle 15°.

questions.questionText: The complex power of a load is S = P + jQ with P positive and Q negative. The load is:
options: Inductive, with a lagging power factor
Capacitive, with a leading power factor
questions.explanation: With S = V I*, a negative Q means the current leads the voltage, which is a capacitive load. The positive P shows it still absorbs active power.

questions.questionText: A workshop takes 45 kW at a power factor of 0.75 lagging from a 400 V single-phase supply. Its kVA demand and line current are:
questions.explanation: S = P/cos φ = 45/0.75 = 60 kVA and I = S/V = 60 000/400 = 150 A. Multiplying by the pf instead of dividing gives 33.8 kVA.

questions.questionText: A 500 kVA transformer is fully loaded. How much additional active power can it supply if the load power factor is raised from 0.7 to 0.9 at the same kVA?
questions.explanation: At 0.7 pf: P = 500 × 0.7 = 350 kW; at 0.9 pf: P = 450 kW. The extra capacity is 450 − 350 = 100 kW with no change in the transformer's current or kVA.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of a low power factor, for the same active power and voltage?
options: More active power is converted into useful work by the load
Larger copper losses in cables and transformers
questions.explanation: The load's active power is the same; a low pf raises the current, which increases I²R losses and voltage drop. It does not give the load more useful power.

questions.questionText: Besides static capacitors, which machine can supply leading reactive power for power-factor correction?
questions.explanation: An over-excited synchronous motor draws leading current, so it behaves like a capacitor; run without load for this purpose it is called a synchronous condenser.

questions.questionText: Power-factor correction in practice is usually stopped at about 0.95 rather than taken to exactly unity because:
options: Unity power factor would make the active power zero
Capacitors cannot supply reactive power at unity power factor
The line current increases as the power factor approaches unity
The capacitor kVAR needed rises steeply near unity for a small further reduction in current
questions.explanation: For 100 kW, going from 0.9 to 0.95 needs about 15.6 kVAR, but 0.95 to 1.0 needs about 32.9 kVAR for only about 5 % less current, so the last step is uneconomical; overshooting also gives a leading pf.

questions.questionText: A pure inductor with X_L = 46 Ω is connected to a 230 V supply. The active and reactive powers are:
questions.explanation: I = 230/46 = 5 A. A pure inductor dissipates no energy, so P = 0, and Q = I²X_L = 25 × 46 = 1150 VAR (lagging).

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 10 Ω and X_L = X_C = 20 Ω is connected to 100 V. The reactive power absorbed by the inductor alone is:
questions.explanation: At X_L = X_C the circuit is resonant: I = V/R = 10 A, so Q_L = I²X_L = 100 × 20 = 2000 VAR. The capacitor supplies an equal 2000 VAR, so the net reactive power from the source is zero.

questions.questionText: A 50 Ω resistor and an inductor of reactance 25 Ω are connected in parallel across a 100 V supply. The power factor is approximately:
questions.explanation: P = V²/R = 200 W and Q = V²/X_L = 400 VAR, so pf = 200/√(200² + 400²) ≈ 0.447. Treating them as a series pair (R/Z = 50/55.9) wrongly gives 0.894.

questions.questionText: A 230 V, 50 Hz single-phase load takes 5 kW at 0.6 pf lagging. The parallel capacitance needed to raise the power factor to unity is approximately:
questions.explanation: Q_C = P tan φ₁ = 5000 × 1.333 = 6667 VAR; C = Q_C/(2πfV²) = 6667/(2π × 50 × 230²) ≈ 401 µF. Using Q = P (5 kVAR) instead gives about 301 µF, and Q = S (8.33 kVA) about 501 µF.

questions.questionText: A 10 kW single-phase load on 400 V operates at 0.707 pf lagging. After a capacitor raises the power factor to 0.9 lagging, the line current falls from about 35.4 A to about:
questions.explanation: I = P/(V cos φ): before, 10 000/(400 × 0.707) ≈ 35.4 A; after, 10 000/(400 × 0.9) ≈ 27.8 A. 25 A would be the current at unity pf.

questions.questionText: A 20 kW load at 0.8 pf lagging has a 25 kVAR capacitor bank connected across it. The resulting power factor is approximately:
questions.explanation: Load Q = 20 × 0.75 = 15 kVAR lagging; net Q = 15 − 25 = −10 kVAR (leading). pf = 20/√(20² + 10²) ≈ 0.894 leading: the bank over-corrects.

questions.questionText: A capacitor bank rated 10 kVAR at 415 V is operated at 380 V with the frequency unchanged. The reactive power it now supplies is approximately:
questions.explanation: Q_C = V²/X_C, so it scales with the square of the voltage: 10 × (380/415)² ≈ 8.38 kVAR. Scaling linearly gives 9.16 kVAR.

questions.questionText: A load has v = 200 sin(314t) V and i = 10 sin(314t − 60°) A. The average power consumed is:
questions.explanation: P = (V_m I_m/2) cos φ = (200 × 10/2) × cos 60° = 1000 × 0.5 = 500 W. Forgetting to convert peak values to rms gives 1000 W.

questions.questionText: A load takes 9 kW at 0.6 pf lagging. Its reactive power is:
questions.explanation: S = P/cos φ = 9/0.6 = 15 kVA, so Q = √(15² − 9²) = 12 kVAR (equivalently P tan φ = 9 × 4/3).

questions.questionText: Which statement about several loads connected to the same AC supply is correct?
options: Their apparent powers always add arithmetically to give the total kVA
Their active powers add, and their reactive powers add algebraically with capacitive VAR taken as negative
Their power factors add to give the overall power factor
Only the active powers add; reactive powers of different loads cannot be combined
questions.explanation: Total P = ΣP and total Q = ΣQ (inductive positive, capacitive negative); the total S = √(P² + Q²) is generally less than the arithmetic sum of the individual kVA.

questions.questionText: For a series RL circuit, which of the following expressions does NOT give the active power?
options: V_R²/R, where V_R is the voltage across R
questions.explanation: Active power is dissipated only in R: P = I²R = VI cos φ = V_R²/R. I²Z = VI is the apparent power in VA.

questions.questionText: Reactive power in an AC circuit represents:
options: Energy converted into heat in the resistance
Power lost permanently in the magnetic core
The peak value of the active power
Energy that flows back and forth between the source and the fields of L and C, with zero average value
questions.explanation: Reactive power measures the rate at which energy is stored and returned by inductors and capacitors each half-cycle; its average over a cycle is zero, so it does no net work.
